Skip to main content SECURITY POLITICS THE BIG STORY BUSINESS SCIENCE CULTURE REVIEWS Newsletters Security Politics The Big Story Business Science Culture Reviews More The Big InterviewMagazineEventsWIRED InsiderWIRED Consulting Newsletters Podcasts Video Livestreams Merch Search Sign In Sign In Emily Mullin Science Jul 27, 2026 5:30 AM Measles Is Becoming So Common That Treatments May Soon Be Needed As the US sees its highest number of measles cases in decades and vaccination rates fall, researchers are developing drugs to help those who contract the virus or who are particularly vulnerable. Photo-illustration: WIRED Staff; Getty Images 8Save this story 8Save this story Up until recently, measles vaccination has been so effective that there’s been little medical or financial incentive to develop treatments for the disease. But as measles cases hit a 35-year high and vaccination rates continue to decline in the US, a handful of biotech companies and academic groups have started working on measles treatments for those infected with the virus as well as vulnerable individuals needing short-term protection. It will likely be years, however, before these countermeasures are available, and it’s even more uncertain if those who refuse vaccines would take such treatments. Fueled by large outbreaks in South Carolina and Utah, the US had already surpassed last year’s 2,289 measles cases, and it’s only July. For comparison, there were just 285 cases in all of 2024. Featured Video Because measles is so contagious, at least 95 percent of people in a community need to receive both doses of the measles vaccine to protect immunocompromised individuals and infants under 12 months old who are too young to be vaccinated. But measles vaccination rates have dipped well below that in many places across the country. Young children are the most susceptible to severe complications from measles. The virus can cause pneumonia by damaging the respiratory tract lining directly and by suppressing the immune system, leaving them susceptible to bacterial infections. It can also cause deafness and potentially fatal brain damage. Without a measles-specific treatment, doctors rely on supportive care such as preventing dehydration, managing breathing difficulties, and administering steroids for inflammation. Vitamin A is sometimes given to patients because the virus can deplete levels of it in the body, but the supplement has no effect on the virus itself. “What we’re seeing now as we get a resurgence of measles in communities is a horrible lack of options when somebody gets exposed,” says Michael Mina, an epidemiologist and chief medical officer of Invivyd, a Connecticut-based biotech company. Invivyd is developing a type of therapy for measles known as a monoclonal antibody, which mimics natural antibodies the immune system makes to fight off disease. Given via IV or injection, monoclonal antibodies were widely used to treat and prevent Covid-19, especially in immunocompromised individuals who didn’t mount a strong immune response to the vaccines. Their protective effects can last up to a few months. Invivyd, which developed a monoclonal antibody for Covid, has been getting inquiries from health care providers about when a similar therapy will be available for measles. In the event of a local measles outbreak, a monoclonal antibody could provide short-term protection to those at high risk of contracting the virus. Invivyd has not yet tested its measles antibody in humans, but Mina says the company is compiling the data needed for the Food and Drug Administration to sign off on clinical trials. At the La Jolla Institute for Immunology, president and CEO Erica Ollmann Saphire has been trying to understand the human antibody response to measles. In May, Saphire and her team published a study describing human antibodies capable of blocking infection by binding to key sites on the measles virus. An infusion of these antibodies resulted in a 500-fold lower viral load in rodents. A key step toward getting these treatments into human trials will be manufacturing monoclonal antibodies at scale, which is a costly and complex process. Clinical trials cost millions of dollars to run, and pharmaceutical partners are usually needed to fund them. But measles treatments could be a hard sell for pharma companies. Drugs for infectious diseases aren’t usually big money-makers because of the sporadic nature of outbreaks and short treatment courses. Most Popular Digital Culture Don’t Get Too Attached to Jimothy By Miles Klee Culture Boomers Can’t Stop Gifting Their Grandkids AI-Generated Slop Books By Miles Klee Space NASA’s New 3D Model Shows the Earth Is a Lumpy Mess By Javier Carbajal Cyberattacks and Hacks OpenAI’s Hacking Debacle Comes Down to Human Error By Lily Hay Newman “I think this is a real opportunity to solve a public health problem,” Saphire says. “A tool by which you could prevent or treat disease is still cheaper than managing an outbreak or managing a case of fatal encephalitis in a child.” Some disease models predict that measles could become endemic in the US in the next 25 years, even at current state-level vaccination rates. Monoclonal antibodies could also be costly for patients and insurers. In early 2022, the US government spent $855 million for 1.7 million doses of Evusheld, a monoclonal antibody treatment authorized for Covid. The medication itself was free to patients, but some people were hit with hundreds of dollars in out-of-pocket costs related to the administration of the drug. The monoclonal antibody combination that became Evusheld was created in just 25 days by scientists at Vanderbilt University, which have also discovered potent antibodies for measles. The university has partnered with small biotech firm Saravir Biopharma to continue development. James Crowe, an immunologist and director of the Vanderbilt Center for Antibody Therapeutics who led the Covid work, says the strategy is to use a combination of two monoclonal antibodies to drastically reduce the chances that the measles virus could mutate to evade it. His group has been systematically making human antibodies against viruses that are most likely to cause future pandemics and happened to be in the middle of the measles work last year when US measles cases intensified. "The antibodies that we have isolated are so potent, they strongly inhibit the virus. We feel for sure they could be formulated as a single, long acting shot,” Crowe says. Once these monoclonal antibodies are ready for human testing, regulators will need to figure out how to evaluate them in clinical trials. New drugs are typically tested in adults first to make sure they’re safe for children. But complications from measles are more likely to hospitalize children, particularly those who are unvaccinated. Antivirals could also be used as a strategy to treat measles, although they tend to be short-lived and must often be given very soon after a person is infected or starts to develop symptoms to be effective. Researchers at Georgia State University identified an oral antiviral drug and tested it in rats, ferrets, and dogs infected with related viruses in the orthoparamyxovirus subfamily since these animals don’t get human measles. The drug lowered viral load and all treated animals survived. It’s not yet been tested in people. A challenge in antiviral development is that drugs toxic enough to kill viruses often have unpleasant side effects for people. The big question, though, is if people will use the treatments being developed or allow their children to take them. While anti-vaccine sentiment is driving the current outbreaks, Mina of Invivyd hopes people who have not vaccinated their children or gotten the vaccine themselves will be open to getting a monoclonal antibody because “this is a molecule that our bodies create naturally.” But during the Utah measles outbreak, some parents have refused to let doctors give their children immune globulin, a broad mix of antibodies derived from donated plasma. And anti-science sentiment has become more mainstream with Robert F. Kennedy Jr. leading the Department of Health and Human Services, where he has cast doubt on vaccines, treatments for depression, and other established medical treatments. That doesn’t mean researching antibodies and other treatments for measles isn’t worth the effort, though, particularly given the potential to help populations who are unable to be vaccinated. Crowe says it’s important that work on measles treatments gets funded as vaccination rates continue to decline. “I think there’s going to be hundreds of thousands of cases,” he says. “People are going to die. There’s some urgency to finishing this work.” Comments (8) Back to top Join the discussion Comments (8) Back to top Join the WIRED community to add comments. The university has partnered with small biotech firm Saravir Biopharma to continue development. James Crowe, an immunologist and director of the Vanderbilt Center for Antibody Therapeutics who led the Covid work, says the strategy is to use a combination of two monoclonal antibodies to drastically reduce the chances that the measles virus could mutate to evade it. His group has been systematically making human antibodies against viruses that are most likely to cause future pandemics and happened to be in the middle of the measles work last year when US measles cases intensified. "The antibodies that we have isolated are so potent, they strongly inhibit the virus. We feel for sure they could be formulated as a single, long acting shot,” Crowe says. Once these monoclonal antibodies are ready for human testing, regulators will need to figure out how to evaluate them in clinical trials. New drugs are typically tested in adults first to make sure they’re safe for children. But complications from measles are more likely to hospitalize children, particularly those who are unvaccinated. Antivirals could also be used as a strategy to treat measles, although they tend to be short-lived and must often be given very soon after a person is infected or starts to develop symptoms to be effective. Researchers at Georgia State University identified an oral antiviral drug and tested it in rats, ferrets, and dogs infected with related viruses in the orthoparamyxovirus subfamily since these animals don’t get human measles. The drug lowered viral load and all treated animals survived. It’s not yet been tested in people. A challenge in antiviral development is that drugs toxic enough to kill viruses often have unpleasant side effects for people. The big question, though, is if people will use the treatments being developed or allow their children to take them. While anti-vaccine sentiment is driving the current outbreaks, Mina of Invivyd hopes people who have not vaccinated their children or gotten the vaccine themselves will be open to getting a monoclonal antibody because “this is a molecule that our bodies create naturally.” But during the Utah measles outbreak, some parents have refused to let doctors give their children immune globulin, a broad mix of antibodies derived from donated plasma. And anti-science sentiment has become more mainstream with Robert F. Kennedy Jr. leading the Department of Health and Human Services, where he has cast doubt on vaccines, treatments for depression, and other established medical treatments. That doesn’t mean researching antibodies and other treatments for measles isn’t worth the effort, though, particularly given the potential to help populations who are unable to be vaccinated. Crowe says it’s important that work on measles treatments gets funded as vaccination rates continue to decline. “I think there’s going to be hundreds of thousands of cases,” he says. “People are going to die. There’s some urgency to finishing this work.” Comments (8) Back to top Join the discussion Comments (8) Back to top Join the WIRED community to add comments. analysis.brief_en: The US is experiencing its highest measles cases in decades, with outbreaks in South Carolina and Utah driving numbers past 2,289 by July 2026—surpassing the total for all of 2024. Declining vaccination rates, falling below the 95% needed for community protection, have reignited interest in treatments. Young children face severe risks, including pneumonia, deafness, and brain damage. Currently, doctors rely on supportive care, but biotech firms like Invivyd are developing monoclonal antibodies similar to those used for COVID-19. These therapies could provide short-term protection for high-risk individuals, though human trials and regulatory approval remain years away. The resurgence highlights a critical gap in preparedness as measles becomes more common.

news.content: You need to enable JavaScript to run this app. Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites Latest videos Latest audio Regions Africa Asia Europe Latin America Middle East North America Germany Topics Climate Equality Health Human Rights Migration Technology Categories Business Science Environment Culture Sports In focus BerlinIranWildfires Latest audioLatest videos Live TV Advertisement ScienceUnited States of America 'Amnesia' about measles risk pushes growth in US infections Richard Connor 07/27/2026July 27, 2026 The latest US data show measles cases from January to mid-July 2026 totaled more than all cases in 2025. Experts blame a fall in vaccination and warn that people have forgotten measles can be life-threatening. https://p.dw.com/p/5HiUO Copy link The measles vaccination is strongly recommended, but some parents are not heeding the callImage: Erin Hooley/Chicago Tribune/TNS/Sipa USA/picture alliance Advertisement Behind the familiar symptoms of fever and spots is an extremely contagious virus that can cause lasting harm or death. That's the reality of measles. But many people in the US appear to have forgotten the seriousness of a measles infection, with outbreaks mainly in under-vaccinated communities. In fact, infections have hit a 35-year high as declining vaccination rates have created growing pockets of susceptible people. Experts warn that the fading memories of the once-common disease have left too many people unaware of its dangers. The number of measles cases in the United States up to mid-July 2026 surpassed the total number of cases in 2025. By the week of July 13-19, 2026, the number of reported measles cases was 2,321. By comparison, the total number of US measles cases in 2025 was 2,286, according to the US Measles Tracker run by the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health. Advertisement What does the rise in measles cases mean? Johns Hopkins epidemiologist William Moss expects the surge in measles cases to result in the US losing the measles-elimination status it has held since 2000. "The significance of reaching this milestone is that the US has not been able to stop measles virus transmission or outbreaks as it has in the past," Moss told DW. Moss said the virus was now spreading "from one susceptible community to another within the US," rather than being limited to infections brought in from abroad. Measles virus is contagious before spots appear Measles is the most contagious virus on Earth, spreading far more easily than the common cold. Nine out of 10 non-immune people exposed to the virus will become infected. Measles spreads through virus-containing droplets released from an infected person's nose, throat and lungs when they breathe, talk or cough. The smallest particles can remain suspended in the air long after the person has left the room. Is the US experiencing a vaccine crisis? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video 05:18 "You just have to be in somebody's airspace within two hours of them being there," said Paul Offit, director of the Vaccine Education Center at the Children's Hospital of Philadelphia. Crucially, people can transmit measles before realizing they are infected. Patients typically become contagious around four days before the characteristic spots or rash appear. The combination of airborne particles, extreme contagion and transmission before obvious symptoms allows the virus to exploit even relatively small gaps in vaccination. Measles complications can emerge years later In the US, about one in five people with measles are hospitalized. One in 20 infected children develops pneumonia, while around one in 1,000 develops encephalitis, a form of brain inflammation that can cause permanent brain damage. Between one and three of every 1,000 infected children die from respiratory or neurological complications. "We had two unvaccinated children — a healthy little six-year-old, a healthy little eight-year-old — die of measles this past year," Offit told DW. Both died with pneumonia. "It's like dying of suffocation," he said. "It's a terrible way to die." Among those who survive, the harm can persist long after the fever and spots disappear. Measles can suppress the immune system for years, erasing some of the protection it had previously developed against other viruses and bacteria. Another delayed complication is subacute sclerosing panencephalitis, a rare but fatal degenerative brain disease that can appear up to 10 years after the original infection. Measles spots spread downward across the body in an easy-to-recognize mannerImage: Alejandro Ernesto/dpa/picture alliance "Children get infected, they get better, they're fine," Offit said. "And then five years later, seven years later, they come in with a deterioration in handwriting skills, deterioration in personality and then they descend into a vegetative state and die." Has the danger of measles been forgotten? Vaccination pushed measles out of everyday life in the US. But that success has also weakened public understanding of why vaccination is necessary. "We've not just largely eliminated measles from our country; we've eliminated the memory of measles," Offit said. "The most serious complications of measles are relatively rare and only become apparent when there is a large number of cases," said Moss. "Unfortunately, the increasing number of measles cases in the US will once again teach us that this is not always a harmless childhood infection." Katelyn Jetelina, an epidemiologist who publishes a Substack newsletter called "Your Local Epidemiologist," said falling vaccination rates reflected a "general amnesia about these diseases," falsehoods on social media and a wider loss of trust in institutions. "The outbreaks remain among under-vaccinated communities," Jetelina said. "There are unvaccinated pockets all around the nation. All it takes is a spark for this disease to spread like wildfire in those pockets." The combination of airborne particles, extreme contagion and transmission before obvious symptoms allows the virus to exploit even relatively small gaps in vaccination. Measles complications can emerge years later In the US, about one in five people with measles are hospitalized. One in 20 infected children develops pneumonia, while around one in 1,000 develops encephalitis, a form of brain inflammation that can cause permanent brain damage. Between one and three of every 1,000 infected children die from respiratory or neurological complications. "We had two unvaccinated children — a healthy little six-year-old, a healthy little eight-year-old — die of measles this past year," Offit told DW. Both died with pneumonia. "It's like dying of suffocation," he said. "It's a terrible way to die." Among those who survive, the harm can persist long after the fever and spots disappear. Measles can suppress the immune system for years, erasing some of the protection it had previously developed against other viruses and bacteria. Another delayed complication is subacute sclerosing panencephalitis, a rare but fatal degenerative brain disease that can appear up to 10 years after the original infection. Measles spots spread downward across the body in an easy-to-recognize mannerImage: Alejandro Ernesto/dpa/picture alliance "Children get infected, they get better, they're fine," Offit said. "And then five years later, seven years later, they come in with a deterioration in handwriting skills, deterioration in personality and then they descend into a vegetative state and die." Has the danger of measles been forgotten? Vaccination pushed measles out of everyday life in the US. But that success has also weakened public understanding of why vaccination is necessary. "We've not just largely eliminated measles from our country; we've eliminated the memory of measles," Offit said. "The most serious complications of measles are relatively rare and only become apparent when there is a large number of cases," said Moss. "Unfortunately, the increasing number of measles cases in the US will once again teach us that this is not always a harmless childhood infection." Katelyn Jetelina, an epidemiologist who publishes a Substack newsletter called "Your Local Epidemiologist," said falling vaccination rates reflected a "general amnesia about these diseases," falsehoods on social media and a wider loss of trust in institutions. "The outbreaks remain among under-vaccinated communities," Jetelina said. "There are unvaccinated pockets all around the nation. All it takes is a spark for this disease to spread like wildfire in those pockets." analysis.brief_en: The United States is experiencing a significant measles outbreak, with cases from January to mid-July 2026 already exceeding the total for all of 2025. Public health experts attribute this surge to declining vaccination rates and what they term 'amnesia' about measles' dangers, as the disease has been largely absent from everyday life since its elimination in 2000. By July 2026, 2,321 cases had been reported, marking a 35-year high. The highly contagious virus is now spreading within the US rather than being limited to imported cases, threatening the country's measles-elimination status. Health officials warn that many people underestimate the severity of measles, which can cause pneumonia, encephalitis, and death, with complications sometimes appearing years after infection.

Alaska wastewater testing samples from Anchorage, Fairbanks, Eagle River and Bethel as they get prepped for processing by the state in July, 2026. Evidence of the measles virus was found in Anchorage wastewater in July, according to state epidemiologists. The data is from a national pilot program that analyzes wastewater for disease and looks for ribonucleic acid, or RNA, of certain pathogens. Joe McLaughlin, head epidemiologist for the state, said that based on those findings, "We've got at least one, maybe several people in the Anchorage sewershed catchment area that had measles around these dates, and we don't know who they were, where they were, or whether transmission was occurring." Wastewater tested positive for evidence of measles on July 7, 8, 9 and 14, but the state doesn't have comparable data yet for dates beyond mid-July. Further data is likely to come in by early August, he said. McLaughlin said officials don't know yet whether the test results are due to a traveler passing through or an Anchorage resident, but clinicians should be vigilant and on the lookout for measles. "Anybody who presents to the urgent care, the emergency department, or in for a routine clinic visit, seeing a child with an acute viral illness that's compatible with measles, they should go ahead and test them and put them in isolation if they think that they do have measles," McLaughlin said. Clayton Weingartner, who heads the wastewater analysis program for the state, said the data is thanks to a new pilot program funded by a national nonprofit organization, which uses a highly sensitive process to analyze Anchorage's wastewater. No other parts of Alaska are included in the pilot program, he said. Alaska analyzes its own wastewater too, through the Department of Environmental Conservation, a lab at the University of Alaska Anchorage and in Bethel through the Yukon-Kuskokwim Health Corporation's Office of Environmental Health. Although state testing is less sensitive, if there are more cases of measles, Weingartner said it would likely show up in the state data too. That testing is analyzed more quickly than the pilot program and can be tracked online. He said the state has detected trace amounts of measles before. "For certain pathogens like measles, which are of such high consequence, we're really working on increasing that (testing) sensitivity," he said and that the state may start notifying the public moving forward if there are trace detections. Weingartner pointed out that a person cannot get measles from wastewater, that it's a respiratory disease. And he said that while people who get the measles vaccine do shed a form of the viral RNA, the testing can differentiate what he called the "wild type" of virus versus the vaccine-derived type. "It's the wild type that we are detecting," he said. The best way to prevent measles transmission is through vaccination, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Typically, children get vaccinated before kindergarten. Symptoms for measles include a rash, high fever, a cough and congestion, tiny white spots in the mouth and red, watery eyes. If you or a family member has symptoms, McLaughlin said it's best to call a clinic before getting tested so they can prevent other patients from being exposed. Measles activity in the United States is at an all-time high since the disease was declared eliminated in the country in 2000. So, McLaughlin said it's really important for Alaskans to take precautions. "Measles could be imported from an Alaskan who's returning to Alaska from the Lower 48, or from abroad, or a tourist," he said. Measles is a very unpleasant disease to get, McLaughlin said, and long-term effects of the illness can include lifelong neurological consequences and occasionally, death. Those most at risk of hospitalization are young children and immunocompromised people. Most elders over age 60, McLaughlin said, were exposed during childhood or later vaccinated, so have immunity to the virus. Immunity through vaccination is lifelong. Evidence of the measles virus was found in Anchorage wastewater in July, according to state epidemiologists. The data is from a national pilot program that analyzes wastewater for disease and looks for ribonucleic acid, or RNA, of certain pathogens. Joe McLaughlin, head epidemiologist for the state, said that based on those findings, "We've got at least one, maybe several people in the Anchorage sewershed catchment area that had measles around these dates, and we don't know who they were, where they were, or whether transmission was occurring." Wastewater tested positive for evidence of measles on July 7, 8, 9 and 14, but the state doesn't have comparable data yet for dates beyond mid-July. Further data is likely to come in by early August, he said. McLaughlin said officials don't know yet whether the test results are due to a traveler passing through or an Anchorage resident, but clinicians should be vigilant and on the lookout for measles. "Anybody who presents to the urgent care, the emergency department, or in for a routine clinic visit, seeing a child with an acute viral illness that's compatible with measles, they should go ahead and test them and put them in isolation if they think that they do have measles," McLaughlin said. Clayton Weingartner, who heads the wastewater analysis program for the state, said the data is thanks to a new pilot program funded by a national nonprofit organization, which uses a highly sensitive process to analyze Anchorage's wastewater. No other parts of Alaska are included in the pilot program, he said. Alaska analyzes its own wastewater too, through the Department of Environmental Conservation, a lab at the University of Alaska Anchorage and in Bethel through the Yukon-Kuskokwim Health Corporation's Office of Environmental Health. Although state testing is less sensitive, if there are more cases of measles, Weingartner said it would likely show up in the state data too. That testing is analyzed more quickly than the pilot program and can be tracked online. He said the state has detected trace amounts of measles before. "For certain pathogens like measles, which are of such high consequence, we're really working on increasing that (testing) sensitivity," he said and that the state may start notifying the public moving forward if there are trace detections. Weingartner pointed out that a person cannot get measles from wastewater, that it's a respiratory disease. And he said that while people who get the measles vaccine do shed a form of the viral RNA, the testing can differentiate what he called the "wild type" of virus versus the vaccine-derived type. "It's the wild type that we are detecting," he said. The best way to prevent measles transmission is through vaccination, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Typically, children get vaccinated before kindergarten. Symptoms for measles include a rash, high fever, a cough and congestion, tiny white spots in the mouth and red, watery eyes. If you or a family member has symptoms, McLaughlin said it's best to call a clinic before getting tested so they can prevent other patients from being exposed. Measles activity in the United States is at an all-time high since the disease was declared eliminated in the country in 2000. So, McLaughlin said it's really important for Alaskans to take precautions. "Measles could be imported from an Alaskan who's returning to Alaska from the Lower 48, or from abroad, or a tourist," he said. Measles is a very unpleasant disease to get, McLaughlin said, and long-term effects of the illness can include lifelong neurological consequences and occasionally, death. Those most at risk of hospitalization are young children and immunocompromised people. Most elders over age 60, McLaughlin said, were exposed during childhood or later vaccinated, so have immunity to the virus. Immunity through vaccination is lifelong. news.content_title: Grandparents for Vaccines advocate for vaccination as Ohio grapples with third Measles outbreak
news.content: CLEVELAND — The Ohio Department of Health (ODH) announced the state’s third measles outbreak of 2026 Thursday, as the nation grapples with surging infection rates. ODH has reported 15 measles cases in 2026. The state had 45 cases in 2025, seven cases in 2024 and one case in 2023. Across the country, the Centers for Disease Control (CDC) is reporting 2,318 cases this year, already surpassing the number of infections for the entire year of 2025. The CDC reports that 93% of the infections in 2026 were in unvaccinated people or individuals with an unknown vaccine status. Measles causes a host of flu-like symptoms including sore throat, cough and fever. It's most recognizable for its blotchy, red rash that spreads from the face down. While many of the people infected recover, the illness can lead to severe complications or even death. “The virus stays in the environment for hours. So if you bring a young child to a pediatrician's office and you're in the waiting room, people who enter that waiting room hours later can contract measles,” Dr. Judith Feinberg, an infectious disease specialist, said. Feinberg is a part of the advocacy group Grandparents for Vaccines, a group of grandparents dedicated to promoting vaccination. “If with a simple vaccination, you could prevent children from being hooked up to a ventilator to breathe or dying from, you know, a fatal brain infection, like to me, that's sort of a no brainer,” Feinberg said. “I have very vivid memories of what life was like before we started vaccinating children,” Mary Koslap-Petraco, another member of Grandparents for Vaccines, said. Koslap-Petraco’s sister was infected with measles when they were children. “I was terrified that she was going to die,” Koslap-Petraco said. “She looked awful. My mother wouldn't even let us in the room with her.” When vaccines became readily available, Koslap-Petraco remembers being thankful. “I used to say, 'wow, I live in a world where parents don't have to worry about losing their children to these horrible diseases,'” Koslap-Petraco said. “Now here I am a dinosaur, thinking to myself, 'oh my God, these poor parents are so afraid of vaccines. They don't know how bad these diseases are.' Am I going to be faced with looking at baby tombstones again?” The measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine provides 97% protection against measles for life, according to the CDC. analysis.brief_en: West Virginia has confirmed its first measles case in over two years, reported in Barbour County by West Virginia Public Broadcasting. The single case marks a significant public health concern as measles is highly contagious and can lead to severe complications, especially in unvaccinated populations. Health officials have not yet released details on potential exposures, contact tracing efforts, or the vaccination status of the affected individual. This outbreak highlights the importance of maintaining high vaccination rates to prevent the spread of measles, which was declared eliminated in the U.S. in 2000 but has seen recent resurgences in areas with low vaccination coverage.

July 30, 2026, 8:16 PM UTC / Source: TODAY Shiv Sudhakar, MD Skip to table of contents 0 seconds of 2 minutes, 18 secondsVolume 0% Press shift question mark to access a list of keyboard shortcuts Keyboard ShortcutsEnabledDisabled Play/PauseSPACE Increase Volume↑ Decrease Volume↓ Seek Forward→ Seek Backward← Captions On/Offc Fullscreen/Exit Fullscreenf Mute/Unmutem Decrease Caption Size- Increase Caption Size+ or = Seek %0-9 Settings OffCCEnglish Font Color White Font Opacity 100% Font Size 100% Font Family Arial Character Edge None Background Color Black Background Opacity 50% Window Color Black Window Opacity 0% Reset WhiteBlackRedGreenBlueYellowMagentaCyan 100%75%50%25% 200%175%150%125%100%75%50% ArialCourierGeorgiaImpactLucida ConsoleTahomaTimes New RomanTrebuchet MSVerdana NoneRaisedDepressedUniformDrop Shadow WhiteBlackRedGreenBlueYellowMagentaCyan 100%75%50%25%0% WhiteBlackRedGreenBlueYellowMagentaCyan 100%75%50%25%0% Auto1080p (4871 kbps)720p (3513 kbps)540p (1768 kbps)360p (956 kbps)270p (499 kbps)270p (278 kbps) Live 00:00 02:18 02:18 Add TODAY to Google RFK Jr. Grilled on Measles Cases, End of Flu Vaccines for Troops 02:18 Create your free profile or sign in to save this article Add TODAY to Google When treating measles patients infected in the Disneyland outbreak that spread to six states and Canada between 2014 and 2015, I learned firsthand that even “the happiest place on Earth” is not immune to a preventable crisis. In fact, many of the urgent public health lessons I took away from this period feel just as relevant as the U.S. battles a 35-year high in measles infections. Last week, the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reported the number of measles cases in 2026 had surpassed 2025’s total, and the nation’s status of having eliminated the virus is at risk, NBC News reported. The chaos that followed the Disneyland outbreak was overwhelming, and the fear of a localized outbreak within the facility where I worked was terrifying. Measles is one of the most contagious viruses on Earth and can cause severe complications. Over a decade later, the short-lived “Disneyland effect” — which temporarily boosted public support for vaccinations — has faded from our collective memory, though it remains vivid in mine. As we face this resurgence, here’s what I want people to know about the measles virus. Your Doctor Probably Has Never Seen a Case of Measles I trained to be an infectious disease specialist. Yet, despite nine years of rigorous medical training, I never encountered a measles case until I was thrown into an outbreak years after graduating. And I’m not alone. With 1 million active physicians in the U.S., the odds of any individual clinician encountering the disease have been incredibly low over the past two decades. Following measles’ U.S. elimination in 2000, the country averaged 100-200 cases annually between 2001 and 2019 (outside of major outbreaks). Research shows this lack of firsthand exposure has created knowledge gaps that could delay making a measles diagnosis. And early diagnosis is important to prevent further spread and complications. Measles Is Not Easy to Diagnose Measles typically begins with non-specific, flu-like symptoms that are easily dismissed as a standard cold until the hallmark rash appears. In medical school, we are taught the “3 Cs” — cough, coryza (runny nose) and conjunctivitis (red eyes) — followed by a blotchy red rash that starts on the face and spreads downward. But when I encountered my first real patient, I almost missed the diagnosis. The only reason I tested for measles was my patient asked me to. Patients are sometimes their best advocate, so don’t be afraid to ask your doctor to order a test or think of diagnosis they may have missed. In its early stages, measles closely resembles many other illnesses. Even a routine allergic reaction to medication can cause a drug rash that looks virtually identical to measles to an untrained eye. Measles Is Not Just a Childhood Rash Measles is a highly contagious disease that can cause ear infections, diarrhea and severe complications in 30% of cases, including: Hospitalization: One in five unvaccinated U.S. patients end up hospitalized. Pneumonia: One out of 20 children develop a lung infection. Brain Swelling: One out of 1,000 children suffer from encephalitis (which can lead to deafness and intellectual disability). Death: The virus kills one to three out of every 1,000 children infected. (There are no documented cases of a healthy, vaccinated person dying of measles.) The risk is highest in children less than 5, adults older than 20, pregnant women, immunocompromised individuals and those with vitamin A deficiency. Measles can also cause complications after recovery. A rare and often fatal central nervous system disease called subacute sclerosing panencephalitis can strike seven to 10 years after the initial infection. Infants under 2 face the highest risk. You Can Still Get Measles If You Are Fully Vaccinated Two doses of the MMR vaccine provide lifelong protection in 97% of people, according to the CDC. An Editor Shares Her Thoughts Deals DealsScore up to 65% off Lululemon’s ‘We Made Too Much’ Section The remaining 3% are susceptible, usually because because their immune systems fail to produce enough antibodies, or intense, prolonged exposure overwhelms their defenses. (Think of living in a confined household where multiple unvaccinated individuals are actively shedding the virus.) But vaccinated individuals who experience breakthrough infections usually suffer a much milder symptoms and are much less likely to transmit the virus to others, research shows. Measles is one of the most contagious viral pathogens on Earth, capable of living in the air for up to two hours after an infected person leaves the room, so if you suspect you have measles, always call a health care facility before showing up so they can take proper isolation protocols. The Measles Vaccine Does Not Cause Person-to-Person Spread The measles vaccine uses a weakened version of the actual virus to safely mimic a natural infection, which results in long-lasting immunity. (It should not be used in immunocompromised people.) I’ve often been asked if a vaccinated person can shed the virus from the vaccine and endanger others, especially immunocompromised folks. Fortunately, the vaccine strain of measles cannot spread from person to person, per the CDC. Vitamin A Is a Supportive Treatment, Not a Cure-All I remember having to tell a measles patient’s mother during the 2015 outbreak that there is no approved antiviral cure, a humbling reminder of our clinical limits. Treatment is strictly supportive: acetaminophen or ibuprofen for fever and pain, aggressive hydration and lots of rest. Vitamin A can also be a supportive treatment, as the measles virus rapidly depletes levels of the nutrient in the blood. During the measles outbreak in Texas last year, the CDC said vitamin A should be given to children hospitalized with severe symptoms. At the same time, the agency also stressed that vitamin A does not prevent infection and is not a replacement for the vaccine. Giving vitamin A also necessitates oversight from a health care provider, since vitamin A toxicity comes with severe risks. The Measles Virus Is More Dangerous Than the Vaccine, Data Show Many patients asked me during the 2015 outbreak if the measles vaccine is safe, and I told them the dangers of catching measles are much greater than the side effects of the vaccine. There are no documented deaths in healthy people due to the measles vaccine, whereas up to three children out of every 1,000 infected with measles will die, according to the Infectious Diseases Society of America. The vaccine can very rarely cause fever-induced seizures — which are not associated with long-term health effects, per the CDC — and immune thrombocytopenic purpura, a rare condition that disrupts blood clotting. ITP is usually not life-threatening and occurs in about one out of 40,000 MMR vaccinations. A measles infection causes severe complications much more often: According to the CDC, about one in 20 children will develop pneumonia and one in 1,000 will develop dangerous swelling of the brain. Shiv Sudhakar, MD Dr. Shiv Sudhakar is a contributing writer for TODAY.com. After writing short stories in medical school, he learned humor really is the best medicine. Being a doctor inspires him to write stories that educate people to learn more about their body and health. As an infectious disease specialist, he has a particular interest in bugs and drugs. He also works in addiction medicine and is passionate about combating homelessness, decreasing substance abuse, improving mental health and elevating extraordinary stories from everyday people. news.source_body_en: As measles cases in the U.S. reach a 35-year high, an infectious disease specialist who treated patients during the 2015 Disneyland outbreak debunks common misconceptions. The article highlights that many clinicians have never seen a measles case due to its rarity since elimination in 2000, potentially delaying diagnosis. Measles is highly contagious, with severe complications including hospitalization (1 in 5 unvaccinated patients), pneumonia (1 in 20 children), encephalitis (1 in 1,000), and death (1-3 per 1,000). While the MMR vaccine is 97% effective, breakthrough infections can occur, though symptoms are milder. The author stresses the importance of early diagnosis and patient advocacy, noting the virus can survive in the air for up to two hours.

news.content_title: Wastewater in Alaska’s largest city signals warning about measles
news.content: The gate to the John M. Asplund Wastewater Treatment Facility is seen on July 29, 2026. The plant serves most o the residents of Alaska's largest city. Wastewater samples taken in early and mid-July revealed genetic material from measles. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon) At least one person in Anchorage had measles in early and mid-July, creating a risk that the highly infectious disease could spread through the state's largest city, state health officials are warning. Samples taken from Anchorage's John M. Asplund Wastewater Treatment Facility revealed genetic material from the strain of measles that has caused outbreaks in the Lower 48. It means someone carrying the virus was in the part of Anchorage served by the state's biggest wastewater treatment plant, said Dr. Joe McLaughlin, Alaska's state epidemiologist. "It doesn't tell us where exactly they were in the sewershed, and it also doesn't tell us if there was any human-to-human transmission that's occurring," he said. But it does provide an early warning to health providers and the general public, McLaughlin said. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. "It's important for people to take a look and see if they've been vaccinated, or if their children have been vaccinated," he said. If children have not been vaccinated, "go ahead and get them vaccinated, because we know that this virus has been present in the community. And it may still be present." The presence of measles RNA, the virus' single-strand genetic material, was detected in samples taken on July 7, 8, 9 and 14, health officials said. State and municipal health officials are still waiting for results from more recent wastewater testing, McLaughlin said. Samples from the Asplund plant are usually taken every Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday, said Clayton Weingartner, the Division of Public Health's wastewater surveillance coordinator. Performing the scan that detects measles genetic material is a complex process, he said. "it's an expensive test, and it takes longer to get the results," he said. That is why state officials are still waiting for results from last week's sampling, he said. For now, public health officials say, Anchorage residents and other Alaskans should be on the lookout for signs of measles . A measles-infected baby being treated in 2014 at a hospital in Manilla, the Philippines capital city, has a rash that is a hallmark symptom of the disease. The Philippines experiencing a large measles outbreak after Typhoon Haiyan, an especially powerful natural disaster. (Photo by Jim Goodson/U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention) Symptoms, which usually arrive a week or two after infection, include a high fever, a runny nose, red eyes and a skin rash. The disease can be serious and even fatal, especially for young children. There were three measles deaths in the United States last year, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. As of Tuesday, there were no new reports of any patients with measles in Anchorage. The last Anchorage case was in October, affecting an adult who tested positive after traveling to the city from the Lower 48, according to municipal officials. There was also a child in Anchorage who was diagnosed with measles in May of 2025. Elsewhere in the state, there were four measles cases diagnosed last year, according to health officials. McLaughlin said there are reasons for Alaskans to be vigilant. There are more measles cases in the United States now than at any time in the past 35 yeas, he said. "And we're at peak tourist season right now, so there are people coming into Alaska from the Lower 48 and from many different countries, and they're bringing with them, some of them, different pathogens," he said. "And one of them can be measles. And we know that measles is the most contagious virus that we're aware of on the planet." Additionally, Alaskans are at elevated risk because the rate of measles vaccination is low compared to the rest of the nation. Medical providers should be notified if there are suspected measles infections, McLaughlin said. Patients should not be in clinic waiting rooms because the virus is so contagious, he said. Whenever a case is identified, health officials have to trace the places where that patient may have exposed others to the virus, such as daycare centers, stores and recreational sites. "All that kind of stuff takes a lot of work, and that's just for one case," he said. Wastewater sampling in Alaska screens for a variety of infectious diseases, including COVID-19, different varieties of influenza and Respiratory Syncytial Virus, or RSV, as well as measles. Numerous sites participate in the National Wastewater Surveillance System , or NWSS, that was set up by the CDC in 2020 as part of the national response to the COVID-19 pandemic. But the Asplund plant, which serves most of Anchorage's residents, is the only one in Alaska that participates in the most advanced testing program, a privately operated system called WastewaterSCAN , Weingartner said. "The WastewaterSCAN program has very limited testing slots," he said. The Alaska Department of Environmental Conservation, the University of Alaska Anchorage and the Yukon Kuskokwim Health Corp. are also testing wastewater for disease pathogens, he said. Samples are regularly collected from wastewater in Eagle River, Juneau and Bethel. news.content_title: Health officials warn of measles outbreak in Ohio
news.content: OHIO — The Ohio Department of Health (ODH) has reported the state’s third measles outbreak of 2026. An outbreak is defined by three or more related cases. ODH said in this latest outbreak three people in Ashtabula County and one in Tuscarawas County are currently infected. All four people were unvaccinated and ranged from 4- to 30-years-old. ODH is working to promote opportunities to get vaccinated and is following up with health departments to follow up on potential exposures. “It’s unfortunate that these outbreaks have become more common in Ohio over the past few years, because this disease is preventable,” ODH Director Dr. Bruce Vanderhoff said. “This serves to emphasize the importance of being fully vaccinated. I strongly encourage you to protect yourselves and your children by getting vaccinated.” Previous outbreaks were reported in January in Cuyahoga County and in February in Franklin County. There have been 15 measles cases so far in 2026. ODH previously reported 45 cases in 2025, seven cases in 2024, and one case in 2023. Measles is extremely contagious and can spread to others through coughing or sneezing. The measles virus can live for up to two hours in the air where an infected person coughed or sneezed. If people breathe contaminated air or touch an infected surface, they can become infected. “The measles vaccine (called MMR as it protects against measles, mumps and rubella) is very safe and effective at preventing measles,” ODH said in a news release. “Two doses of MMR is 97% effective against measles. If you are up to date on the measles vaccine, the risk of getting sick is very low.” Symptoms include rash, high fever, runny nose, cough, loss of appetite, and red, watery eyes. The rash usually lasts five to six days and begins at the hairline before moving to the face and upper neck and then down the body. For more information about measles, visit ODH’s website

news.excerpt: Samples taken from a plant in the state’s largest city revealed genetic material from measles, a highly contagious disease that is particularly dangerous for young children.

news.content_title: Wastewater in Anchorage signals warning about measles
news.content: Research professional Nate Beck prepares a sample of wastewater from the Asplund Wastewater Treatment Plant so that it can be tested for SARS-CoV-2 on Feb. 6, 2024 at the University of Alaska Anchorage. Wastewater sampling in Alaska screens for a variety of infectious diseases, including COVID-19, different varieties of influenza and respiratory syncytial virus, or RSV, as well as measles. (Loren Holmes / ADN archive) At least one person in Anchorage had measles in early and mid-July, creating a risk that the highly infectious disease could spread through the state’s largest city, state health officials are warning. The proof is in the sewage . Samples taken from Anchorage’s John M. Asplund Wastewater Treatment Facility revealed genetic material from the strain of measles that has caused outbreaks in the Lower 48. It means someone carrying the virus was in the part of Anchorage served by the state’s biggest wastewater treatment plant, said Dr. Joe McLaughlin, Alaska’s state epidemiologist. “It doesn’t tell us where exactly they were in the sewershed, and it also doesn’t tell us if there was any human-to-human transmission that’s occurring,” he said. But it does provide an early warning to health providers and the general public, McLaughlin said. “It’s important for people to take a look and see if they’ve been vaccinated, or if their children have been vaccinated,” he said. If children have not been vaccinated, “go ahead and get them vaccinated, because we know that this virus has been present in the community. And it may still be present.” The presence of measles RNA, the virus’s single-strand genetic material, was detected in samples taken on July 7, 8, 9 and 14, health officials said. State and municipal health officials are still waiting for results from more recent wastewater testing, McLaughlin said. Samples from the Asplund plant are usually taken every Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday, said Clayton Weingartner, the Division of Public Health’s wastewater surveillance coordinator. One of six clarifiers at the AWWU Asplund Wastewater Treatment Facility at Point Woronzof on Dec. 10, 2024. (Bill Roth / ADN) Performing the scan that detects measles genetic material is a complex process, he said. “It’s an expensive test, and it takes longer to get the results,” he said. That is why state officials are still waiting for results from last week’s sampling, he said. For now, public health officials say, Anchorage residents and other Alaskans should be on the lookout for signs of measles . Symptoms, which usually arrive a week or two after infection, include a high fever, a runny nose, red eyes and a skin rash. The disease can be serious and even fatal, especially for young children. There were three measles deaths in the United States last year, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. As of Tuesday, there were no new reports of any patients with measles in Anchorage. The last Anchorage case was in October, affecting an adult who tested positive after traveling to the city from the Lower 48, according to municipal officials. There was also a child in Anchorage who was diagnosed with measles in May of 2025. Elsewhere in the state, there were four measles cases diagnosed last year, according to health officials. McLaughlin said there are reasons for Alaskans to be vigilant. There are more measles cases in the United States now than at any time in the past 35 years, he said. “And we’re at peak tourist season right now, so there are people coming into Alaska from the Lower 48 and from many different countries, and they’re bringing with them, some of them, different pathogens,” he said. “And one of them can be measles. And we know that measles is the most contagious virus that we’re aware of on the planet.” Additionally, Alaskans are at elevated risk because the rate of measles vaccination is low compared to the rest of the nation. Medical providers should be notified if there are suspected measles infections, McLaughlin said. Patients should not be in clinic waiting rooms because the virus is so contagious, he said. Whenever a case is identified, health officials have to trace the places where that patient may have exposed others to the virus, such as daycare centers, stores and recreational sites. “All that kind of stuff takes a lot of work, and that’s just for one case,” he said. Wastewater sampling in Alaska screens for a variety of infectious diseases, including COVID-19, different varieties of influenza and respiratory syncytial virus, or RSV, as well as measles. Numerous sites participate in the National Wastewater Surveillance System , or NWSS, that was set up by the CDC in 2020 as part of the national response to the COVID-19 pandemic. But the Asplund plant, which serves most of Anchorage’s residents, is the only one in Alaska that participates in the most advanced testing program, a privately operated system called WastewaterSCAN , Weingartner said. “The WastewaterSCAN program has very limited testing slots,” he said. The Alaska Department of Environmental Conservation, the University of Alaska Anchorage and the Yukon Kuskokwim Health Corp. are also testing wastewater for disease pathogens, he said. Samples are regularly collected from wastewater in Eagle River, Juneau and Bethel. news.content: Facebook-f X-twitter Envelope Subscribe Home About 49th State Lower 48 Top News Commentary Northern Ledger Intel 907 Juneau Story Features and events Donate Home About 49th State Lower 48 Top News Commentary Northern Ledger Intel 907 Juneau Story Features and events Donate Home » Measles virus detected in Anchorage wastewater; no recent human cases confirmed 49th State, Top News Measles virus detected in Anchorage wastewater; no recent human cases confirmed Listen By THE ALASKA STORY July 27, 2026 – Measles virus RNA was detected in several Anchorage wastewater samples collected earlier this month, prompting Alaska public health officials to alert healthcare providers Monday. The Alaska Section of Epidemiology said the virus was found in samples collected July 7, 8, 9 and 14. The concentrations were described as “very low,” and no recent human case of measles has been confirmed in Alaska. The finding does not establish that measles is spreading in Anchorage, but it indicates that the virus was present somewhere within the Anchorage sewer system during the July 7–14 period. The Anchorage sewershed includes the city and Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson but does not include Eagle River or Girdwood. WastewaterSCAN, a national disease-surveillance program, notified state epidemiologists July 22 and 24 after metagenomic sequencing detected the viral genetic material. Wastewater testing can detect viruses, bacteria and other substances shed through toilets, sinks, showers, laundry and drains. It cannot identify the person who carried the virus, establish whether that person was an Anchorage resident or visitor, or determine whether community transmission is occurring. State officials emphasized that people cannot contract measles from wastewater. Measles is a respiratory disease that spreads through the air when an infected person coughs, sneezes or breathes. The detection comes as the United States experiences its highest measles case count in 35 years. As of July 23, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention had recorded 2,318 confirmed cases during 2026, already exceeding the 2,289 cases reported during all of 2025. Thirty-five new outbreaks have been reported this year, and 93% of confirmed cases have been linked to outbreaks, according to the CDC. Alaska epidemiologists instructed healthcare providers to remain alert for patients with possible measles, particularly those with recent domestic or international travel, contact with travelers, or incomplete or unknown vaccination histories. Early symptoms can include fever, cough, runny nose and red, watery eyes. Small white spots known as Koplik spots may develop inside the mouth, followed by a red rash that usually begins on the face and spreads downward across the body. Providers who suspect measles are being instructed to place the patient in airborne isolation immediately and notify the Section of Epidemiology at 907-269-8000. The after-hours number is 800-478-0084. Officials said providers should not wait for laboratory confirmation before reporting a suspected case. State health officials are also encouraging Alaskans to check whether they are current on their measles, mumps and rubella vaccinations. Children generally receive two doses of the MMR vaccine, while adults without evidence of immunity should consult a healthcare provider. The CDC says two doses provide the best protection and usually provide lifelong immunity against measles. The wastewater results are not presently displayed on the public WastewaterSCAN dashboard because they were discovered through metagenomic sequencing rather than the standard digital droplet PCR testing used for publicly reportable concentration levels. WastewaterSCAN has indicated that sequencing results may be added to the dashboard in the future. WastewaterSCAN, a national disease-surveillance program, notified state epidemiologists July 22 and 24 after metagenomic sequencing detected the viral genetic material. Wastewater testing can detect viruses, bacteria and other substances shed through toilets, sinks, showers, laundry and drains. It cannot identify the person who carried the virus, establish whether that person was an Anchorage resident or visitor, or determine whether community transmission is occurring. State officials emphasized that people cannot contract measles from wastewater. Measles is a respiratory disease that spreads through the air when an infected person coughs, sneezes or breathes. The detection comes as the United States experiences its highest measles case count in 35 years. As of July 23, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention had recorded 2,318 confirmed cases during 2026, already exceeding the 2,289 cases reported during all of 2025. Thirty-five new outbreaks have been reported this year, and 93% of confirmed cases have been linked to outbreaks, according to the CDC. Alaska epidemiologists instructed healthcare providers to remain alert for patients with possible measles, particularly those with recent domestic or international travel, contact with travelers, or incomplete or unknown vaccination histories. Early symptoms can include fever, cough, runny nose and red, watery eyes. Small white spots known as Koplik spots may develop inside the mouth, followed by a red rash that usually begins on the face and spreads downward across the body. Providers who suspect measles are being instructed to place the patient in airborne isolation immediately and notify the Section of Epidemiology at 907-269-8000. The after-hours number is 800-478-0084. Officials said providers should not wait for laboratory confirmation before reporting a suspected case. State health officials are also encouraging Alaskans to check whether they are current on their measles, mumps and rubella vaccinations. Children generally receive two doses of the MMR vaccine, while adults without evidence of immunity should consult a healthcare provider. The CDC says two doses provide the best protection and usually provide lifelong immunity against measles. The wastewater results are not presently displayed on the public WastewaterSCAN dashboard because they were discovered through metagenomic sequencing rather than the standard digital droplet PCR testing used for publicly reportable concentration levels. WastewaterSCAN has indicated that sequencing results may be added to the dashboard in the future. Arizona is part of one of the nation's largest measles outbreaks as the number of cases surpasses the record high set in 2025, with five more months of 2026 still to come. A report from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention cites more than 2,318 cases so far this year — the highest number in more than 30 years. Most of that is attributable to several major outbreaks, including a recent surge on the Arizona-Utah border. Experts have used mathematical modeling and genetic analyses to indicate the outbreak on the Utah-Arizona border could be around three to four times bigger than what’s currently known, Utah epidemiologist Dr. Leisha Nolen said. Health officials say that’s because some infections likely go unreported. The nation had 2,289 cases in 2025, the worst year for measles in more than three decades. Now, 2026 has easily become the U.S.’s worst year for measles since 1991. In addition to the significant outbreak in Utah and Arizona, an outbreak of measles in South Carolina and smaller clusters of cases in other states have sickened hundreds. In November, international health officials will meet to determine if the U.S. and Mexico have lost their measles-free status. The U.S. eliminated local measles spread in 2000 by maintaining high vaccination rates, which have fallen in recent years to below the 95% coverage needed to prevent outbreaks. Measles cases are undercounted While measles cases in the U.S. are climbing, it may be impossible to say exactly how far-reaching the spread is. Public health departments and disease researchers have long acknowledged that official counts are incomplete, because some people get sick and don’t seek out treatment — something not unique to measles. Furthermore, experts say the spread might be greater than what’s known because the virus is one of the most contagious known to medicine and vaccination rates nationwide have declined. National vaccination rates for measles, mumps and rubella — which dropped to 92.5% among kindergartners in the 2024-25 school year, from 95.2% in 2019-20 — obscure even lower rates in certain communities. In Utah, where public health officials have fought measles for more than a year, the virus has sickened more than 700 people during that time, according to the state health department. The picture is muddier in South Carolina, which had the nation’s largest outbreak in 35 years. There, the 997 total is likely an undercount, the state health department has said, but it doesn’t know by how much. KNAU and Arizona News Measles virus detected in Sedona wastewater samples Bree Burkitt , July 14, 2026 Samples from the Sedona Wastewater Treatment Plant tested positive for the measles virus. That indicates that at least one person with a recent infection has been in the area. Listen • 0:43 Dr. Brannon Traxler, acting director of the state department of health, said the undercount is “impossible to know and may vary during the course of an outbreak.” Data gaps can make it hard to reliably estimate an outbreak’s true scope. Experts say hospitalization rates can be a good barometer, but measles hospitalizations are not required to be reported in every state. “If we really had some kind of solid gold standard for the percentage of all cases that have hospitalization or some measure of severity, then that would be another way of estimating the outbreak size that we could see if it’s consistent with these other methods,” said Damon Toth, an applied mathematician at the University of Utah’s medical school who is working on one of the Utah outbreak analyses. Researchers are still analyzing the 2025 Texas outbreak In Texas, researchers are still working to estimate the size of the state’s 2025 outbreak and early findings show it might have been nearly twice the size of the 762 known cases. Rémy Pasco, a mathematical epidemiologist at the University of Colorado Boulder who is working on the analysis, said the undercounts were unsurprising. In the absence of an adequate community vaccination rate — 95% according to health experts — “there’s just not much you can do about measles once you have it,” he said. The CDC defines an outbreak as three or more linked cases. But by the time three such cases are identified in communities with low vaccination rates and less disease surveillance, “either you missed the previous ones or you’re going to have a lot more,” he added. Dr. Varun Shetty, Texas’ chief state epidemiologist, said there were instances where people tested positive for measles but health officials couldn’t confirm who else was in the person’s household or if they were sick. “What we’re able to count and report is almost always an underestimate of what actually occurred, because it relies on people being willing to be able to get tested, to share information with healthcare providers and with public health,” Shetty said. “Sometimes that just doesn’t happen.” The state health department previously reported that 182 probable measles cases went unconfirmed in March 2025 among minors in Gaines County — the epicenter of the outbreak — due to a lack of information. The confirmed case count for the western Texas county for the whole outbreak is 414. Shetty expects to keep seeing measles cases and even outbreaks because so many people are unprotected. “It’s really critical, not only for individual people, but for communities, to have high vaccination coverage,” he said. Vaccination is about protecting others, physician says Dr. Mark Roberts, retired director of the Public Health Dynamics Lab at the University of Pittsburgh School of Public Health, worries most for the people he calls “innocent bystanders.” Research and measles modeling by his team shows those who cannot get vaccinated — young babies, people with weak immune systems and those who rarely don’t get robust immunity from the vaccine — bear the brunt of outbreaks early on. Some people see skipping vaccination as like deciding not to wear a seat belt in a car, Roberts said. “Not vaccinating your kid is like saying, ‘I don’t want my car to have brakes,’” he said. “Because it’s other people that you can hit. It’s not just you in your car. news.content_title: North Bay health officials warn of national measles uptick, stress importance of vaccination
news.content: Sarah White comforts her 20 month-old son Landden as he receives the MMR vaccine for measles, mumps and rubella from Maribel Gonzalez, a medical assistant team leader at Santa Rosa Community Health, Tuesday, July 28, 2026, in Santa Rosa. (Kent Porter / The Press Democrat) By Martin Espinoza | martin.espinoza@pressdemocrat.com | The Press Democrat PUBLISHED: July 29, 2026 at 7:04 AM PDT | UPDATED: July 30, 2026 at 2:20 PM PDT Getting your Trinity Audio player ready... Lea el artículo en español aquí. Amid a record rebound of measles cases across the country, North Bay health officials and medical professionals are urging parents to follow the advice of physicians and heed science — not internet-fueled fears — in making important vaccination decisions. While the vast majority of parents in Sonoma and Napa counties have elected to have their children vaccinated against a number of infectious diseases, vaccine hesitancy has left pockets of the nation increasingly vulnerable, according to health experts. The federal Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reported last week that U.S. measles cases had hit 2,318 this year so far, more than any recorded year since the disease was declared eliminated in 2000. It’s also more than the 2,289 cases reported in all of 2025. Last year, two unvaccinated children in Texas died of measles-related acute respiratory failure. John Swartzberg, an infectious disease expert at UC Berkeley, said the rise of the anti-vaccine movement, coupled with the Trump administration’s attempts to scale back childhood vaccine recommendations, have resulted in a “marked decline” in the number of people getting vaccinated. “The consequences of that are that that we’ve seen measles re-emerge,” Swartzberg said. “Last year, we had two children die of measles...this year we’re having even more cases. Fortunately we haven’t seen any deaths this year.” Dr. Mia Shim, Sonoma County’s new health officer, called the national trend deeply concerning, given that today’s outbreaks could have been prevented had the country stayed the course it was on a quarter century ago. “The vaccination status in these outbreaks tells an important story,” Shim said. “93% of people who were infected with measles in these outbreaks were unvaccinated.” Shim said the vast majority of today’s outbreaks in the United States have been caused by unvaccinated U.S. residents traveling and then bringing the disease back into local communities where immunization rates have fallen below the 95% threshold that protects the community. When immunization rates fall below that level, the disease can spread very quickly, Shim said. Maribel Gonzalez, a medical assistant team leader at Santa Rosa Community Health, draws up a vaccine, Tuesday, July 28, 2026, in Santa Rosa. (Kent Porter / The Press Democrat) A singles dose vaccine for measles, mumps and rubella at Santa Rosa Community Health, Tuesday, July 28, 2026, in Santa Rosa. (Kent Porter / The Press Democrat) Vaccines ready to be delivered at Santa Rosa Community Health, Tuesday, July 28, 2026, in Santa Rosa. (Kent Porter / The Press Democrat) 1 of 3 Maribel Gonzalez, a medical assistant team leader at Santa Rosa Community Health, draws up a vaccine, Tuesday, July 28, 2026, in Santa Rosa. (Kent Porter / The Press Democrat) Expand Swartzberg said declining vaccination rates have set back the country’s campaign against measles a generation. “We’re back to where we were 30 years ago,” he said. Highly contagious Measles hasn’t been in circulation in Sonoma County since 1993, according to local health officials. The last confirmed case in the county, in 2011, was a traveler from Europe. A case in Napa County, tied to domestic U.S. travel, was confirmed back in January. In the early 1990s, U.S. cases were far fewer than they’ve been in the past two years. By decade, the nation averaged hundreds of thousands of cases in the early to mid-1960s; tens of thousands through the seventies; thousands in the 1980s and hundreds for most the 1990s. Measles was declared eliminated in the U.S. — but not eradicated — in 2000. That meant there was no longer any measles spreading within the country and all new cases were from people contracting the virus abroad. Now, that’s no longer the case, said Dr. Christine Wu, Napa County’s public health officer. “We live in a society where we’re not staying put, we love to travel, especially people in California,” said Wu. “And now it’s not just traveling abroad that can bring measles back into communities but travel within the United States. To me that’s a big concern ahead of school coming back into session.” This table shows the number of measles cases by month that have been detected in California so far in 2026. Source: California Department of Public Health Wu said there are communities in the state as well as Napa County where there’s been an increase in preventable illnesses for which vaccines are available, including whooping cough or pertussis, tetanus, “things you don’t even think about anymore.” For many people today, the seriousness of measles is somewhat of an abstraction. Today’s young parents weren’t alive when U.S. cases numbered in the hundreds of thousands every year. For their parents, however, the disease was well known: In 1962, a year before the measles vaccine was licensed, there were 482,530 cases, according to the CDC. Dr. Irene Baluyut, a pediatrician and chief medical informatics officer at Santa Rosa Community Health, said you don’t have to dig through U.S. medical journals or archived news stories to get some idea of what America’ s pre-vaccination era was like. Baluyut said there are many parts of the world where measles is still a problem. “I grew up in the Philippines and I’ve seen measles,” Baluyut said. “I’ve seen how devastating it is. I’ve seen how fast it travels.” Baluyut said the measles virus is far more contagious than say the influenza or COVID-19 viruses. She said measles can stay airborne and active in a room for up to two hours after an infected person leaves the space. After it has gained hold in an environment shared by unvaccinated people, she said, it spreads very quickly. Children are the most vulnerable to measles-related illnesses, particularly infants under 12 months. Dr. Shim, the Sonoma County health officer stressed that being vaccinated protects infants who may not have received all their shots yet, as well as older people with weakened immune systems who may not be able to receive the vaccine. “Getting vaccinated is one of the important ways we care for one another and prevent measles transmission,” Shim said. Swartzberg, the UC Berkeley infectious disease expert, said measles was historically a serious childhood disease before the vaccine and there was no effective way to treat it. “We just accepted it as something we went through during childhood,” he said, adding that most people survived infection but in some cases there were “tragic consequences.” Measles The measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccine is extremely effective and provides a lifetime of protection. Two doses provide 97% protection against measles. Measles is very contagious. Measles spreads when someone infected speaks, coughs, sneezes or breathes. It can linger in the air up to two hours after the infected person has left. Unvaccinated people are at high risk. Roughly 90% of those unvaccinated and exposed to measles will contract the disease. ​​ Source: California Department of Public Health Getting measles The virus that causes measles enters the “respiratory tree” and mainly causes respiratory symptoms, such as red eyes, runny nose and cough, Swartzberg said. However, the virus also goes throughout the body and can affect people’s immune system, making them susceptible to other infectious diseases for months to even a few years, he said. “But it also affects our central nervous system,” he said. According to the CDC, one of every 1,000 measles infections can lead to brain inflammation or encephalitis, usually within days or weeks of the measles rash appearing. Swartzberg said in such cases measles illness can harm vital parts of the nervous system, including hearing and visual damage. “It can also lead to more serious and more diffuse neurological problems, some of which can be fatal,” he said. “That’s the nervous system component that people often don’t recognize.” Many health health experts trace much of the hesitancy back to a 1998 study by a British physician that claimed a link between the MMR vaccine and autism . That study was entirely debunked and exposed as an elaborate hoax. The Lancet, the medical journal that published the study, fully retracted it after an extensive investigation. Britain’s General Medical Council then stripped the study’s author, Andrew Wakefield, of his medical license. Dr. Adrienne Silver, a pediatrician and director of medical education at Kaiser Permanente Santa Rosa, said she believes parents’ vaccine hesitancy is “fear-based” or “emotion-based.” “If you Google something, you’re going to find something,” she said, referring to the ease with which misinformation can spread. “It’s a decision based on what-if, what if it’s my child,” she said. “Parents want to do the right thing by their children and they worry...it’s really a heartfelt fear that much of the misinformation plays on.” Silver said that no medication is without some level of risk. “If you take Tylenol there’s a risk of an allergic reaction,” she said. “There’s always some degree of risk in almost everything we do, but when you look at the risk benefit, the risks are so much more rare than the benefit of the vaccine.” You can reach Staff Writer Martin Espinoza at 707-521-5213 or martin.espinoza@pressdemocrat.com.
