analysis.time: Publication date: July 29, 2026 (updated July 30, 2026). Event timeframe: National measles cases reported through July 2026, with historical context dating back to the 1960s.
analysis.location_and_population: United States, with specific focus on North Bay region (Sonoma and Napa counties, California). Affected population: Unvaccinated individuals, particularly children under 12 months and communities with immunization rates below 95%.
analysis.event: Confirmed national measles resurgence with 2,318 cases reported in 2026 (as of last week), exceeding the previous year's total of 2,289 and marking the highest annual count since measles was declared eliminated in 2000. Health officials attribute this to declining vaccination rates and urge adherence to physician recommendations.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: Cases: 2,318 nationally in 2026 (exceeding 2025's 2,289). Deaths: Two unvaccinated children died of measles-related acute respiratory failure in 2025; no deaths reported in 2026 as of publication. Risk: High due to measles' extreme contagiousness (can remain airborne for up to two hours) and rapid spread in communities with vaccination rates below the 95% threshold.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: Health officials (Sonoma County Health Officer Dr. Mia Shim, Napa County Public Health Officer Dr. Christine Wu, UC Berkeley expert Dr. John Swartzberg) are emphasizing vaccination importance and addressing vaccine hesitancy. Investigation ongoing regarding specific outbreak sources. Uncertainty exists about future transmission as school resumes. Historical context provided: measles eliminated in U.S. in 2000 but now circulating domestically again.

analysis.brief_en: Health officials across the United States are sounding alarms as measles cases reach a 26-year high, with 2,318 cases reported in 2026 alone—more than in any year since the disease was declared eliminated in 2000. In California's North Bay region, doctors and public health leaders are urging parents to follow scientific evidence and vaccinate their children, noting that 93% of recent infections occurred in unvaccinated individuals. The highly contagious virus, which can remain airborne for hours, poses particular risks to infants and those with weakened immune systems. While two unvaccinated children died from measles complications in 2025, no fatalities have been reported this year yet. Health experts attribute the resurgence to declining vaccination rates, exacerbated by the anti-vaccine movement and policy changes, warning that communities with immunization rates below 95% are vulnerable to rapid outbreaks.

(WJAC) — A measles case has been reported in the region, according to the Pennsylvania Department of Health, which confirmed that it is a single case in Bedford County. While no further details about the patient or potential exposures were immediately provided, state health officials say they are working to conduct contact tracing of the infected individual. Measles is a highly contagious, vaccine-preventable virus that spreads through the air and can cause serious illness. The Bedford County case brings Pennsylvania’s total reported measles cases to 158. Skip to main content HOME NEWS Gov & Politics Environment Health Education Justice Transportation Work & the Economy Commentary ABOUT SUBSCRIBE DONATE Part of States Newsroom Search Search Gov & Politics Environment Health Education Justice Transportation Work & the Economy 1:42 News Story Health Health experts: State’s high vaccination rate is keeping spread of measles in check Maryland’s 96% vaccination coverage prevents further spread, as outbreaks in other states put unvaccinated residents at risk By Danielle J. Brown - July 28, 2026 1:42 am Maryland health officials and public health experts urge Marylanders to vaccinate against measles amid nationwide surge in cases. (Photo by Jerry Saslav/U.S. Air Force) Just seven months into the year, confirmed measles cases in Maryland are already four times higher than they were for all of last year, but health officials say the situation could be much worse. Almost all of the 12 cases recorded so far this year — up from three for all of 2025 — were “imported” into Maryland after out-of-state or international travel. But once here, the infections have not spread further, which experts say is a sign that the state’s relatively high vaccine coverage at 96% is protecting residents from the potentially fatal illness. “This is higher than many previous years, but it doesn’t represent sustained transmission within Maryland,” said Dr. William Moss, director of the International Vaccine Access Center at Johns Hopkins University. “We have now had repeated importations into the state without sustained transmission.” It’s a trend that he and public health officials hope to protect amid growing vaccine skepticism as new state data shows more parents opting their children out of required school vaccinations. Approximately 96% of Marylanders have lifelong protection from measles due to being vaccinated, above the national average of 93%, according to data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Other Marylanders who have already been sick with measles are also considered immune. The recommend vaccination coverage rate to considered necessary to protect a community from measles is 96%, but as regions across the United States struggle with outbreaks, the dozen cases identified in Maryland reflect those challenges. Of the 12 cases identified by the Maryland Department of Health this year, nine were detected after the resident returned from out-of-state travel, while two cases were detected after international travel. The most recent case, announced June 23 by the health department, did not indicate where the individual may have picked up measles. But Moss says that the lack of sustained community transmission is “a signal of the strength of our immunization program and our really good measles vaccine coverage.” That coverage may be slipping, as more Maryland families cite religious reasons to opt their kids out of vaccinations that are otherwise required to enter kindergarten through religious exemptions. The Maryland Department of Health reports that during the 2025-2026 school year, 2.1% of kindergartners had religious exemptions from the vaccinations, up from 1.7% the year before. That’s more than 1,300 of the 65,500 kindergartners enrolled in the 2025-2026 school year. It’s the highest percentage since 2019-2020, when the religious exemption rate was 2.7% amid disruptions in the school year due to COVID-19. That said, overall vaccine coverage among kindergarteners was still at least 95% in every Maryland county, even in counties where religious exemptions were higher like Allegany and Worcester, according to the health department’s most recent data. “High vaccination rates in schools are crucial for preventing outbreaks and maintaining community immunity,” the Maryland Department of Health said in a written statement Monday. “Maryland maintains a strong safety net with 96.7% of kindergarteners reported as vaccinated in the 2025-2026 school year.” Dr. Andrea Berry is an associate professor of pediatrics at the University of Maryland School of Medicine and a pediatric infectious disease specialist at University of Maryland Golisano Children’s Hospital. She says that over the last few years, there’s been growing confusion and vaccine skepticism among parents, which leads them to opt their kids out of vaccines, including the measles vaccine. “There is a very close relationship between vaccination rates and the likelihood of an outbreak,” she said. “Overall, Maryland does a really great job getting children vaccinated, but the increase in these exemptions stems from vaccine hesitancy.” Meanwhile, the number of measles cases climbs across the United States with 2,318 cases confirmed as of July 23 this year. Those cases have reached 44 states and Washington, D.C., with Maryland’s neighbors among the states with the largest measles outbreaks currently, with Virginia facing 176 measles cases and Pennsylvania facing 134 cases. Measles cases have reached a 35-year high, CDC reports Despite Virginia’s high vaccination rate at 96%, the measles outbreak it’s facing occurred in two rural counties where vaccination rates are less than 75%. Meanwhile, Pennsylvania’s statewide vaccination rate is 92%. Moss warns that the growing measles cases in neighboring states create a greater chance of exposure when Marylanders are visiting those regions, especially in communities with lower vaccination coverage. He says Maryland is “not immune to having local transmission.” “I suspect that we have communities here in Maryland that have lower vaccine coverage ... but fortunately, these imported cases have not made it into those communities yet,” he said. “Traveling to a place where there’s ongoing measles virus transmission ... the most important thing is to make sure you’re protected against measles.” Berry noted that anyone past the age of 6 months can get a measles vaccination. She urges Marylanders to get vaccinated if they are not already protected through prior illness from measles, especially as cases rise in neighboring states. “Now that there are so many outbreaks all throughout the United States, it’s more likely that somebody is going to travel to those places or speak to somebody who did travel those places,” she said. “With the vaccine, you’re much less likely to get measles, and when people do get measles, it is not as severe.” 1 X Republish Post Health experts: State’s high vaccination rate is keeping spread of measles in check by Danielle J. That coverage may be slipping, as more Maryland families cite religious reasons to opt their kids out of vaccinations that are otherwise required to enter kindergarten through religious exemptions. She says that over the last few years, there’s been growing confusion and vaccine skepticism among parents, which leads them to opt their kids out of vaccines, including the measles vaccine.

“There is a very close relationship between vaccination rates and the likelihood of an outbreak,” she said. “Overall, Maryland does a really great job getting children vaccinated, but the increase in these exemptions stems from vaccine hesitancy.”

Meanwhile, the number of measles cases climbs across the United States with 2,318 cases confirmed as of July 23 this year. Those cases have reached 44 states and Washington, D.C., with Maryland’s neighbors among the states with the largest measles outbreaks currently, with Virginia facing 176 measles cases and Pennsylvania facing 134 cases.

Measles cases have reached a 35-year high, CDC reports

Despite Virginia’s high vaccination rate at 96%, the measles outbreak it’s facing occurred in two rural counties where vaccination rates are less than 75%. Meanwhile, Pennsylvania’s statewide vaccination rate is 92%.

Moss warns that the growing measles cases in neighboring states create a greater chance of exposure when Marylanders are visiting those regions, especially in communities with lower vaccination coverage. He says Maryland is “not immune to having local transmission.”

“I suspect that we have communities here in Maryland that have lower vaccine coverage ... but fortunately, these imported cases have not made it into those communities yet,” he said. “Traveling to a place where there’s ongoing measles virus transmission ... the most important thing is to make sure you’re protected against measles.”

Berry noted that anyone past the age of 6 months can get a measles vaccination. She urges Marylanders to get vaccinated if they are not already protected through prior illness from measles, especially as cases rise in neighboring states.

“Now that there are so many outbreaks all throughout the United States, it’s more likely that somebody is going to travel to those places or speak to somebody who did travel those places,” she said. “With the vaccine, you’re much less likely to get measles, and when people do get measles, it is not as severe.”

news.content: News Sports Entertainment Lifestyle Real Estate Advertise Obituaries eNewspaper Legals NEWS Ohio reports 3rd measles outbreak of 2026; US cases hit 35-year high Chad Murphy USA TODAY NETWORK July 31, 2026, 2:23 p.m. ET Ohio is currently experiencing its third measles outbreak of 2026, with all infected individuals being unvaccinated. The latest Ohio outbreak includes four infected individuals in Ashtabula and Tuscarawas Counties. Nationwide, measles cases have reached a 35-year high, surpassing totals from the previous year. Health officials attribute the rise in cases to declining vaccination rates, which have fallen below the 95% threshold for herd immunity. Ohio is reporting its third measles outbreak of 2026 as cases nationwide hit a 35-year high for a disease once declared eradicated in the United States. The latest outbreak, defined as three or more related cases, includes four infected individuals — three in Ashtabula County and one in Tuscarawas County — ranging in age from 4 to 30, the Ohio Department of Health announced July 30. All four were unvaccinated. “It’s unfortunate that these outbreaks have become more common in Ohio over the past few years, because this disease is preventable,” Dr. Bruce Vanderhoff, ODH director, said a statement. “This serves to emphasize the importance of being fully vaccinated. I strongly encourage you to protect yourselves and your children by getting vaccinated.” Nationwide, data released July 22 by the Johns Hopkins University shows 2,295 measles cases have been reported nationwide so far this year, surpassing the 2,286 infections recorded during all of 2025 and marking the highest annual total since 1991, USA TODAY reports. Measles cases in Ohio growing So far in 2026, ODH is reporting 15 measles cases and two previous outbreaks – three cases in Cuyahoga County in January and seven cases in Franklin County in February, according to the state's Summary of Infectious Diseases dashboard. Measles cases have been growing in Ohio over the past several years, with 45 in 2025, seven cases in 2024 and one case in 2023. Measles cases hit 35-year high in United States The United States declared measles eliminated in 2000 after recording just 86 cases that year, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, USA TODAY reports. But a series of outbreaks that began in early 2025, centered initially in Gaines County, Texas, has helped drive the virus' resurgence. Health experts say the recent surge has been fueled by declining vaccination rates that have left more communities vulnerable to outbreaks. Why are measles cases on the rise? Ohio vaccination rates Vaccination for measles has declined in recent years, resulting in a growing number of states no longer reporting rates consistent with herd immunity. Herd immunity occurs when more than 95% of people in a community are vaccinated and most people are protected, even if they cannot get the vaccine themselves, because those around them are immune and cannot spread the disease. Vaccination coverage among U.S. kindergartners decreased from 95.2% during the 2019–2020 school year to 92.5% in the 2024–2025 school year, well under the threshold necessary for effective herd immunity, according to the CDC. Declining protections have also been attributed to the growing anti-vaccine movement, which was bolstered by the confirmation of vaccine skeptic Robert F. Kennedy Jr. as health secretary. In addition to making anti-vaccine comments, Kennedy also downplayed pediatric deaths related to measles and touted false cures and preventives, such as the use of vitamin A. During the height of the Texas outbreak, Kennedy encouraged inoculation against measles, pulling back from his previous anti-vaccine messaging. In Ohio, MMR vaccine — which protects against measles, mumps and rubella — coverage rate for children and adolescents was 91.5% for 2023, the most recent year available from ODH. Previous years ranged from an 80% to 90% immunization rate: 2019: 81.8% 2020: 88.0% 2021: 91.7% 2022: 89.0% Two doses of MMR are 97% effective against measles, ODH reports. If you are up to date on measles vaccine, the risk of getting sick is very low. Are measles deadly? Symptoms Measles can be deadly. ODH states that complications from measles are more common among children younger than 5 years of age, adults older than 20 years of age, pregnant women, and people with compromised immune systems. As many as one out of every 20 children with measles gets pneumonia, the most common cause of death from measles in young children. Symptoms include a rash, high fever, runny nose, cough, loss of appetite and red, watery eyes. The rash usually lasts five to six days and begins at the hairline, moves to the face and upper neck, and proceeds down the body. Diarrhea and ear infections are common complications of measles. More severe complications such as pneumonia and encephalitis, a swelling of the brain, may also occur. The measles virus can live for up to two hours in air where an infected person coughed or sneezed. If other people breathe the contaminated air or touch an infected surface and then touch their eyes, noses, or mouths, they can become infected. People infected with measles can spread it to others from four days before, through four days after, a rash appears. How to protect yourself against measles Both ODH and the CDC say the best way to protect yourself against measles is to be vaccinated. USA TODAY reporters James Powel and Mary Walrath-Holdridge contributed to this report. Fresh Air Wild Card with Rachel Martin It's Been a Minute Embedded Get NPR+ More Podcasts & Shows Search Newsletters NPR Shop Get NPR+ Sign InPersonalize Your Experience Tiny Desk New Music Friday All Songs Considered Music Features Live Sessions About NPR Diversity Support Careers Press Ethics More than 2,000 measles cases reported in the U.S. so far, outpacing 2025's total NPR's A Martinez asks Dr. Jennifer Nuzzo of Brown University why there have been more measles cases this year so far than in all of last year, and what can be done to stop the resurgence. Health More than 2,000 measles cases reported in the U.S. so far, outpacing 2025's total July 27, 20264:40 AM ET Heard on Morning Edition A Martínez More than 2,000 measles cases reported in the U.S. so far, outpacing 2025's total Listen· 3:473-Minute ListenPlaylist Transcript Toggle more options Download Embed Embed <iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/nx-s1-5906455/nx-s1-9864190" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player"> Transcript NPR's A Martinez asks Dr. Jennifer Nuzzo of Brown University why there have been more measles cases this year so far than in all of last year, and what can be done to stop the resurgence. Transcript A MARTÍNEZ, HOST: There are more than 2,300 confirmed cases of measles in the U.S. so far this year. That is slightly more than the total number of cases for all of last year, according to the CDC. Dr. Jennifer Nuzzo has been tracking this year's spike in measles. She's an epidemiologist who heads the Pandemic Center at the Brown University School of Public Health. Dr., measles was officially eliminated from the U.S. in 2000. How did this resurgence happen? JENNIFER NUZZO: Well, we've been seeing a slow progress towards measles circulating again because people are, you know, not vaccinating their kids as much as they used to be. But really, it's taken off quite extraordinarily since the beginning of 2025. And some of that is because of a lot of rhetoric right now that's been happening politically about vaccines and suggesting that they may not be safe, which is not true, suggesting that they may not work, which is definitely not true. And that has led to explosive outbreaks throughout the country - recurring outbreaks - to the point where we are now looking at measles being reestablished as a disease that kids could get if they're not vaccinated. MARTÍNEZ: So you expect the U.S. will lose that eliminated status? NUZZO: By all measure, we should lose that status. Measles has continued to be transmitted since the beginning of 2025. It shows no signs of stopping. States that had an outbreak that burnt itself out have seen outbreaks again. It's basically like Whac-A-Mole at this point. MARTÍNEZ: All right. And just to be clear, eliminated means a disease has gone from a region, eradicated it means it's a global - it's gone completely, right? NUZZO: Yeah, it basically means you drive your domestic transmission down to zero. We still had measles when we - since we eliminated it in the year 2000, but they were sporadic cases imported when people traveled to other places. MARTÍNEZ: Why is this resurgence in measles cases so serious? NUZZO: Well, measles is a really terrible disease. You don't want to get measles, you don't want your children to get measles. First of all, it's a deadly disease. It kills, you know, a decent number of people. It puts a lot of people in the hospital, and that's bad for everybody. It's bad for the people who are there with measles. It's also bad for patients who now have a hospital that has to deal with the stress of measles. It's bad for societies because it costs tens of thousands of dollars per measles case. And if your child has measles as a toddler and recovers, you still have to worry about a very rare but fatal complication that can occur as much as a decade later. And that's a really terrible state to be in. MARTÍNEZ: If someone is vaccinated from the measles or their whole families are vaccinated, are they safe? Are they OK? NUZZO: Yeah, so the great thing about the measles vaccine is it's one of the best vaccines we have. It's one of the safest vaccines we have. It's also one of the most effective. And it really does a great job of keeping people from getting sick with measles, certainly keeping people out of the hospital, keeping them from dying, which is the most important thing, but it does a pretty great job of reducing transmission, and that's how we have been able to eliminate it more than 25 years ago. MARTÍNEZ: The Senate is considering the nomination of Dr. Erika Schwartz to lead the CDC. Her boss would be Health Secretary RFK Jr. He's pushed some conspiracy theories about vaccines. Quickly, Dr., if you can, if she is confirmed - if Dr. Schwartz is confirmed - what does she have to do to reverse the rise of measles? NUZZO: She has to issue an unequivocable statement that supports measles vaccination as the only way to protect people from measles - that it's the only proven way to protect yourself from measles. We can't mince words here. We can't suggest that there are, you know, more cons than there are pros. None of that is true. And unfortunately, you know, confusing rhetoric coming out of the Department of Health and Human Services has complicated the issue in the midst of a deadly outbreak. MARTÍNEZ: Dr. Jennifer Nuzzo directs the Pandemic Center at the Brown University School of Public Health. Dr., thanks. NUZZO: Thanks so much. (SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC) Copyright © 2026 NPR. Health More than 2,000 measles cases reported in the U.S. so far, outpacing 2025's total July 27, 20264:40 AM ET Heard on Morning Edition A Martínez More than 2,000 measles cases reported in the U.S. so far, outpacing 2025's total Listen· 3:473-Minute ListenPlaylist Transcript Toggle more options Download Embed Embed <iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/nx-s1-5906455/nx-s1-9864190" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player"> Transcript NPR's A Martinez asks Dr. Jennifer Nuzzo of Brown University why there have been more measles cases this year so far than in all of last year, and what can be done to stop the resurgence. Transcript A MARTÍNEZ, HOST: There are more than 2,300 confirmed cases of measles in the U.S. so far this year. That is slightly more than the total number of cases for all of last year, according to the CDC. Dr. Jennifer Nuzzo has been tracking this year's spike in measles. She's an epidemiologist who heads the Pandemic Center at the Brown University School of Public Health. Dr., measles was officially eliminated from the U.S. in 2000. How did this resurgence happen? JENNIFER NUZZO: Well, we've been seeing a slow progress towards measles circulating again because people are, you know, not vaccinating their kids as much as they used to be. But really, it's taken off quite extraordinarily since the beginning of 2025. And some of that is because of a lot of rhetoric right now that's been happening politically about vaccines and suggesting that they may not be safe, which is not true, suggesting that they may not work, which is definitely not true. And that has led to explosive outbreaks throughout the country - recurring outbreaks - to the point where we are now looking at measles being reestablished as a disease that kids could get if they're not vaccinated. MARTÍNEZ: So you expect the U.S. will lose that eliminated status? NUZZO: By all measure, we should lose that status. Measles has continued to be transmitted since the beginning of 2025. It shows no signs of stopping. States that had an outbreak that burnt itself out have seen outbreaks again. It's basically like Whac-A-Mole at this point. MARTÍNEZ: All right. And just to be clear, eliminated means a disease has gone from a region, eradicated it means it's a global - it's gone completely, right? NUZZO: Yeah, it basically means you drive your domestic transmission down to zero. We still had measles when we - since we eliminated it in the year 2000, but they were sporadic cases imported when people traveled to other places. MARTÍNEZ: Why is this resurgence in measles cases so serious? NUZZO: Well, measles is a really terrible disease. You don't want to get measles, you don't want your children to get measles. First of all, it's a deadly disease. It kills, you know, a decent number of people. It puts a lot of people in the hospital, and that's bad for everybody. It's bad for the people who are there with measles. It's also bad for patients who now have a hospital that has to deal with the stress of measles. It's bad for societies because it costs tens of thousands of dollars per measles case. And if your child has measles as a toddler and recovers, you still have to worry about a very rare but fatal complication that can occur as much as a decade later. And that's a really terrible state to be in. MARTÍNEZ: If someone is vaccinated from the measles or their whole families are vaccinated, are they safe? Are they OK? NUZZO: Yeah, so the great thing about the measles vaccine is it's one of the best vaccines we have. It's one of the safest vaccines we have. It's also one of the most effective. And it really does a great job of keeping people from getting sick with measles, certainly keeping people out of the hospital, keeping them from dying, which is the most important thing, but it does a pretty great job of reducing transmission, and that's how we have been able to eliminate it more than 25 years ago. MARTÍNEZ: The Senate is considering the nomination of Dr. Erika Schwartz to lead the CDC. Her boss would be Health Secretary RFK Jr. He's pushed some conspiracy theories about vaccines. Quickly, Dr., if you can, if she is confirmed - if Dr. Schwartz is confirmed - what does she have to do to reverse the rise of measles? NUZZO: She has to issue an unequivocable statement that supports measles vaccination as the only way to protect people from measles - that it's the only proven way to protect yourself from measles. We can't mince words here. We can't suggest that there are, you know, more cons than there are pros. None of that is true. And unfortunately, you know, confusing rhetoric coming out of the Department of Health and Human Services has complicated the issue in the midst of a deadly outbreak. MARTÍNEZ: Dr. Jennifer Nuzzo directs the Pandemic Center at the Brown University School of Public Health. Dr., thanks. NUZZO: Thanks so much. (SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC) Copyright © 2026 NPR. analysis.time: Publication date: July 27, 2026. Event timeframe: Cases reported so far in 2026, with transmission continuing since the beginning of 2025.
analysis.location_and_population: Affected population: Unspecified general population, with outbreaks recurring in multiple states.
analysis.event: Confirmed measles outbreak with over 2,300 cases reported so far in 2026, exceeding the total for all of 2025. Reported by NPR, citing CDC data. The outbreak is described as a resurgence with potential loss of the U.S. measles elimination status.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: Cases: Over 2,300 confirmed cases in 2026 (slightly more than the total for 2025). Impact: Measles described as a deadly disease causing hospitalizations and deaths. Risk: High, with ongoing transmission and potential reestablishment of endemic measles in unvaccinated populations.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: Investigation and tracking by epidemiologist Dr. Jennifer Nuzzo of Brown University. Response includes calls for clear public health messaging supporting vaccination. Uncertainty exists regarding political rhetoric affecting vaccine uptake and the potential impact of new leadership at the CDC.

analysis.brief_en: The United States is experiencing a significant measles resurgence with over 2,300 confirmed cases reported so far in 2026, exceeding the total for the previous year. According to CDC data cited by NPR, this outbreak represents a potential loss of the U.S. measles elimination status achieved in 2000. Epidemiologist Dr. Jennifer Nuzzo attributes the surge to declining vaccination rates fueled by political misinformation about vaccine safety and efficacy. Measles, a highly contagious and potentially fatal disease, is causing hospitalizations and straining healthcare systems. The outbreak is characterized by recurring outbreaks across multiple states with no signs of stopping. Public health experts emphasize that vaccination remains the most effective prevention method, though confusing messaging from health officials has complicated response efforts.

Amelia was born and raised in Dallas, Texas, and graduated from John Paul II High School. Read Full Bio Amelia Mugavero July 29, 2026 / 10:34 PM CDT / CBS Texas Add CBS News on Google North Texas doctors are urging parents to check their children's measles vaccination records before school starts, as the U.S. faces its worst measles outbreak in more than 30 years. Just weeks before students return to classrooms, measles – a virus once considered eliminated in the United States – is making a comeback. More than 2,300 cases have been reported nationwide this year, the highest count since 1991, and four cases were confirmed in Texas this week. Internal medicine physician Dr. David Winter with Baylor Scott & White says measles spreads with extraordinary ease. "It's said to be the most contagious virus on the planet," Winter said. CBS News Texas He warns that the illness can be severe for children. "If a child gets the measles, about a third of them will get very, very sick. Very sick," Winter said. "The death rate can be up to 5-10% in kids." Winter says declining vaccination rates are a major factor behind the rise in cases. "The vaccine is safe for children," Winter said. "So, in my view, all children should be vaccinated. It's a preventable disease." Doctors say the biggest concern is when measles reaches communities with lower vaccination rates – and new state data shows some North Texas districts are falling below recommended levels. About 93 percent of Texas kindergarteners were fully vaccinated against measles last school year, but several districts fell short. Dallas ISD's MMR vaccination rate for kindergarteners was about 82 percent, while Denton, Celina, and LoveJoy ISDs were all below 90 percent. Health experts generally recommend about 95 percent immunity in a community to help prevent outbreaks. Dallas County Health Director Dr. Philip Huang points to a recent outbreak as a reminder of the stakes. "Last year, in West Texas, there was a record measles outbreak just in Texas, and, you know, and there were two child deaths," Huang said. "And, you know, that should wake people up on how this is really serious. And, so, you know, getting these messages out." Huang says the MMR vaccine takes about two weeks to provide protection, meaning parents shouldn't wait until the first day of school to make sure their children are up to date. Symptoms can appear within days after exposure and may include moderate fever, cough, runny nose, red eyes, and sore throat. "It's a safe and effective vaccine that's worked for decades, and it's a reason why the United States declared measles eliminated in 2000, and now we're really backtracking on it," Huang said. analysis.brief_en: North Texas doctors are urging parents to ensure their children are vaccinated against measles before the school year begins, as the U.S. faces its worst measles outbreak in over 30 years. With over 2,300 cases reported nationwide this year—the highest since 1991—and four confirmed in Texas this week, health officials emphasize the virus's extreme contagiousness and severity. Measles, once eliminated in the U.S., is making a comeback, with declining vaccination rates cited as a key factor. In North Texas, some school districts fall below the recommended 95% immunity threshold, raising concerns about potential outbreaks. Doctors warn that one-third of infected children may become severely ill, with a death rate of 5-10%. Health authorities stress the importance of timely vaccination, as it takes about two weeks for protection to take effect.

news.content: News Sports Autos Business Michigan Life + Home Entertainment Opinion Obituaries MICHIGAN Michigan health officials urge vaccinations as measles threat looms Anne Snabes The Detroit News July 30, 2026, 12:57 p.m. ET Hear this story View Comments Michigan health officials on Thursday urged families to check their vaccination records and catch up on missed vaccines ahead of the school year as the United States logs the most measles cases in 35 years and a comeback of whooping cough is happening. Michigan has seen 14 cases of measles this year, most of which were associated with outbreaks in Washtenaw and Ottawa counties, and the state confirmed 30 cases in 2025. But the state isn't fully through 2026 yet, said Ryan Malosh, director of the Division of Immunization at the Michigan Department of Health and Human Services. "There's still opportunities for there to be additional cases," Malosh said. At a virtual roundtable on Thursday, Dr. Natasha Bagdasarian, the state's chief medical executive, said the U.S. is experiencing the worst year for measles since 1991. She said the country's number of measles cases this year has already surpassed the total for 2025. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said 2,318 confirmed measles cases had been reported in the U.S. this year as of July 23. Measles is a very contagious virus and can cause serious health complications, the CDC said. The I Vaccinate campaign, a public-private partnership that provides parents with information about vaccinations, held the roundtable on Thursday with health officials and advocates for vaccination. As the start of the school year approaches, Bagdasarian urged parents to check their children's vaccination records to ensure they don't have any outstanding immunizations and asked them to follow the American Academy of Pediatrics' immunization schedule. Rachel VanDenBrink, a Kent Intermediate School District nurse consultant and Michigan Director of the National Association of School Nurses, said that when families choose to vaccinate, the impact "reaches far beyond a single shot." "It protects ... your student from severe illness and lost learning time," VanDenBrink said. "It creates a safe environment in the school for vulnerable classmates who have chronic health conditions and rely on that community immunity to attend school safely. It protects the younger siblings at home who are still too young to be fully vaccinated." Measles in Michigan this year Michigan saw outbreaks of measles earlier this year, including an outbreak with seven cases in Washtenaw County and one with four cases in Ottawa County, according to the state health department. The state has also reported three cases this year that weren't associated with outbreaks: two in Macomb County and one in Monroe County. Malosh said Michigan has not seen "a lot of activity" since the spring. "Through the dedicated efforts of our local health department staff ― really, I mean, hours and hours and hours of staff time dedicated to controlling these outbreaks ― we were able to minimize the impact, and we haven't seen many additional cases this year," he said. Malosh said the state confirmed 30 cases of measles in 2025, but it didn't report any in each year from 2019 through 2024. But in 2018, Michigan reported around 38 or 39 cases, he said. Vaccination rates have declined About 76% of kids in Michigan in the preschool age group ― 19- to 35-month-olds ― have received the recommended doses of the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine, Malosh said. This represents an about 10% drop over the last five years, he said About 70% of kindergarten-aged kids in Michigan have had the two recommended doses of MMR vaccine, Malosh said. This tends to mean children ages 4 and 5 years old. Bagdasarian also noted that pertussis, or whooping cough, is "making a comeback." news.source_body_en: Michigan health officials are urging families to ensure vaccinations are up-to-date as the state faces a measles outbreak with 14 confirmed cases in 2026. This comes as the U.S. reports its highest measles cases in 35 years, with 2,318 cases confirmed as of July 23. Michigan has seen outbreaks in Washtenaw and Ottawa counties, with additional cases in Macomb and Monroe counties. Health officials emphasize the importance of vaccination as rates have declined, with only 76% of preschoolers and 70% of kindergarteners fully vaccinated for MMR. The state successfully controlled recent outbreaks but warns that additional cases are still possible. Officials are promoting vaccination through the I Vaccinate campaign as the school year approaches.

news.content_title: Florida ranks 5th in the country for the most measles cases
news.content: ORLANDO, Fla. — Florida ranks fifth in the nation for the most measles cases, according to data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. On July 24, the CDC announced the highest number of cases the country has seen since 1992. Dr. Hernando Cardona, who runs Pediatrics of Greater Orlando, said he hasn’t seen a case of measles at his clinic, but he witnessed the disease while working in Colombia. “It was pretty bad,” he said. “Most cases don’t go into encephalitis or anything like this, but when it does, it’s bad.” Florida has a lower rate of vaccination than most states, with 88.8% of kindergarteners inoculated against measles in 2025, according to the CDC’s most recent data. The CDC recorded 141 cases in Florida near the end of July. “I am an advocate for the vaccine, but if some families don’t want to do the vaccine, it’s well within their rights,” Cardona said. Florida Surgeon General Joseph Ladapo was in Orlando on July 24 and spoke about the outbreak in Collier County. He emphasized people’s right to exemptions but backed the vaccine. “This one happens to be effective against measles, and people should be able to have the information about the vaccine and about the disease and be able to come to a decision without any coercion,” he said. Orange County has only seen four cases in the past 10 years, according to Florida Department of Health data , but three were confirmed in the past 12 months. Cardona said the first dose children get when they’re around 12 months old is 93% effective, and the second dose they get going into kindergarten is 99% effective

Add Axios on Google Data: CDC; Map: Sara Wise / Axios Virginia is one of the seven states accounting for the majority of U.S. measles cases as kids prepare to head back to school. Why it matters: The nationwide measles case count has officially shattered last year's record, hitting levels unseen in more than three decades, according to CDC data released Friday. The big picture: Virginia has reported at least 177 measles cases, per the latest state Department of Health update Tuesday. That is 35 times higher than the total recorded for 2025: five cases. It's also the fourth-highest case count recorded among states, trailing only Texas (803), South Carolina (670) and Utah (197). Zoom in: Nearly every case in Virginia is among unvaccinated people, and most (66%) are minors. And although Central Virginia is a hotspot, there haven't been any measles cases reported in the Richmond area. The outbreaks, so far, are largely in Buckingham and Cumberland. By the numbers: The CDC recommends two doses of the measles vaccine for children by age 6 and a 95% vaccination coverage rate for the highest level of protection against spread. But recent VDH data updated last week shows the two-dose rate for 5-year-olds statewide is only 72% — though the rate rises to 87% by age 7. It's far lower in Buckingham and Cumberland counties for both age groups. Among rates for 5-year-olds in the region, Richmond (85%), Goochland (78%), Henrico (73%) and Chesterfield (73%) are above 70% — a change from earlier this year when only the city and Petersburg were above that threshold. Some of the lowest rates: Hanover (65%) and Petersburg (69%). Both are lower than the rates reported in February. The intrigue: First-dose coverage in Virginia remains much higher, a pattern that's continued with about 95% of 5-year-olds meeting that mark statewide, per VDH. Locally, Richmond, Henrico, Petersburg and Goochland are the only ones to hit that same 95% coverage. Reality check: The biggest risk remains for unvaccinated people and communities with lower vaccination rates, but health officials have advised residents to skip large, crowded events in areas having outbreaks. analysis.brief_en: Virginia is experiencing a significant measles outbreak, with 177 confirmed cases as of July 23, 2026—a 35-fold increase from the previous year. The state ranks fourth nationally in measles cases, trailing only Texas, South Carolina, and Utah. Nearly all cases involve unvaccinated individuals, with 66% affecting minors. The outbreak is concentrated in Buckingham and Cumberland counties, though Richmond remains unaffected. Nationwide, measles cases have reached a 30-year high. Health officials emphasize the importance of vaccination, noting Virginia's two-dose coverage for 5-year-olds is 72%, well below the CDC's recommended 95% for optimal protection. Residents in outbreak areas are advised to avoid large gatherings.

Add Axios on Google Illustration: Lindsey Bailey/Axios Measles cases are surging in Pennsylvania and across the U.S. to levels not seen in years. Why it matters: The virus is rebounding in communities with lower vaccination rates. The big picture: The U.S. has reported at least 2,318 measles cases as of late last week — a 35-year record. The majority of cases are among unvaccinated people. None of Pennsylvania's cases this year have involved people who were fully vaccinated. By the numbers: Pennsylvania has reported 142 measles cases through yesterday — far surpassing last year's total (16). That's the state's highest annual total in at least 25 years. The previous high was 17 cases in 2019, the state health department tells Axios. Pennsylvania has recorded 26 hospitalizations and no deaths this year. Zoom in: Lancaster County is the epicenter of Pennsylvania's outbreak, accounting for roughly 60% of cases. The county also has some of the state's lowest student vaccination rates. Other measles hotspots include Lebanon County (20 cases) and Chester County (14 cases). Meanwhile, Philadelphia, Delaware and Bucks counties have no reported cases. Between the lines: Pennsylvania's student vaccination rate was estimated at 92.4% last year, per the CDC — below the herd immunity threshold of 95% that public health authorities say is necessary to contain the virus' spread. Zoom out: The U.S. has confirmed measles cases across 45 jurisdictions —South Carolina, Utah, Texas, Florida and Arizona have the most reported cases. The last time the U.S. recorded more measles cases was in 1991, with 9,643 cases, according to CDC data. Threat level: Measles symptoms include a cough, high fever and conjunctivitis as well as a telltale rash. But symptoms can escalate into complications such as severe ear infections, pneumonia and encephalitis or inflammation of the brain that can lead to permanent brain damage and even death, per Johns Hopkins Medicine. analysis.time: Publication date: 2026-07-30; Event date: 2026-07-30.
analysis.location_and_population: Northern California; specific census tracts with measles vaccination coverage below the herd immunity threshold; affected population: residents of those tracts.
analysis.event: Kaiser Permanente Division of Research reports a study that identifies clusters of measles vulnerability in Northern California, confirming that certain census tracts have vaccination coverage below the herd immunity threshold.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: No specific case or death counts are reported, but the identified low‐coverage areas pose a heightened risk for measles outbreaks.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The study highlights the vulnerability but does not detail immediate public health actions; further investigation and targeted vaccination efforts are implied.

analysis.brief_en: Kaiser Permanente’s Northern California Division of Research released a study on July 30, 2026, revealing clusters of measles vulnerability across specific census tracts in the region. The analysis shows that vaccination coverage in these areas falls below the herd immunity threshold, creating a heightened risk for measles outbreaks. While the report confirms the existence of low‐coverage pockets, it does not provide case or death statistics, nor does it outline immediate public health interventions. The findings suggest a need for further investigation and potentially targeted vaccination campaigns to close coverage gaps and mitigate outbreak risk. The study is an official scientific assessment, offering a data‐driven basis for future public health planning.

By Rachel Grubbs Published: Jul. 30, 2026 at 10:12 PM UTC|Updated: 23 hours ago Share Add Us On GoogleAdd as a preferred source on Google CAPE GIRARDEAU, Mo. (KFVS) - In less than a month, Heartland students will be back in classrooms. As parents check off items on back-to-school shopping lists, health officials want them to remember to squeeze in routine checkups. That includes making sure students are up to date on vaccinations. It’s something Illinois and Missouri both require before children go to school, including immunization against measles. CDC officials say there have been more reported measles cases so far in 2026 than all of last year. It’s a record-breaking number, more than 2300. It’s also the highest number reported in the U.S. in decades. Amber Grant with the Cape Girardeau County Public Health Center said the measles virus is highly contagious. “It is airborne, so just being in the room with somebody and breathing the same air causes a chance for that person to be able to contract that illness.” People can receive vaccinations, including the MMR vaccine, through the Cape County Public Health Center. They’re offered Monday through Friday during open hours, 8:30 a.m. to 4 p.m. New this year, Grant said they’re offering a drive-through vaccine clinic on Wednesdays. “They do not even have to get out of their car. They just drive around. We’re able to review that immunization record and discuss with them what vaccines they’re due for and then go from there.” Grant said physicals are a chance to catch things early, including abnormalities with hearing or vision and curves in the spine. It’s especially important for young athletes, who may need injury accommodation. “In addition, they can listen to their heart, their lungs, see if there’s any kind of concerns there that might require further followup. They can kind of get just a good head-to-toe assessment to see if there’s any concerns that they need to think about for that school year.” The public health center is located 1121 Linden St. in Cape Girardeau. news.content: ROCHESTER, N.Y. — First day of school is just right around the corner, and medical professionals are advising parents to not overlook an important step before walking the halls at schools — vaccines. What You Need To Know Measles is one of the most contagious viruses in the country — affecting anyone, but most commonly within children As medical experts report the virus surpasses an alarming benchmark, measles has made its resurgence and is having doctors become more worrisome this time around There have been nine reported cases of measles in New York outside of New York City so far this year For parent Jennifer Rodriguez, she is getting a head start on preparing her son for the back-to-school season from social skills to playtime and most importantly staying vigilant on the most up to date immunizations. “Jacob is going to be 14 months old in a couple days,” Rodriguez said. “Like every other parent, first-time parents, we're always worried about everything, especially vaccines. So, I always tend to ask my pediatrician how safe it is. And he always reassures me that it's safe and that they're very important, especially during the winter and the pneumonia, COVID [and] flu. So he has all his shots, so he is healthy. And yeah, all the shots are up to date. As a parent, why is it so important for your kids to have vaccines, not only for his own protection, but also for, like, other kids, I really believe in the science.” Measles has continued a historic resurgence across the United States. “I was like terrified because I always want to bring him outside [and] have him play with other kids [and] socialize,” Rodriguez said. “But you just never know. Especially how bad of a virus measles is like. It can cause brain damage or even death. Especially when you see the recent like rising cases because of people not wanting to vaccinate recently. And it's very scary, especially when he grows up and starts going to school, being around other kids. And I just want him to be as protected as he can.” Going into its record breaking second year in a row, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reports there has been 2,318 confirmed cases across the country, marking its highest number in 35 years. “It is very concerning for me as an infectious disease specialist, as a pediatrician, as a mother of children, and as someone who really cares and worries about the community I live in,” SUNY Upstate Medical University pediatrics professor Dr. Jana Shaw said. Medical professionals say the alarming cases are due to misinformation and lack of vaccinations. “Confidence in vaccination among public declines is misinformation or disinformation, essentially intentional spread of false information about vaccines,” Shaw said. “The reason why this is worrisome is unlike, for some, measles may be perceived as a mild infection. And just the opposite is true. Measles is a very serious childhood infection. It's a virus that is highly contagious. It will find children and adults who are not immune. The infection occurs, rather quickly, after exposure. And those symptoms may not be initially recognized by healthcare professionals because we been lucky and fortunate to see measles essentially eliminated in the United States since 2000. But what it also means [is] that most of the younger healthcare professionals and parents have not seen measles, and as such, they may not be aware of the infection and may not think of the infection, which further leads to propagation transmission in our communities.” And although no deaths have been reported so far, the disease can still be fatal. “The reason why we vaccinate is because we don't know ahead of time which children or adults will go and develop serious complications pneumonia, dehydration, brain infection, seizures [or] death,” Shaw said. “We don't know ahead of time. Even healthy children die from measles. Sometimes they may go on developing seizures that leads to a vegetative state. There's no cure for this condition and is fatal. It kills all the people who end up with this complication. So I'm mentioning all those details not to alarm or scare anyone, but to simply highlight that measles is not a benign or an infection. Not to fear. In fact, it's an infection that can have complications, can be very serious, can land children into hospital, and can also kill. And as such, it's really important that as parents, when they choose not to vaccinate, they understand that risk because unfortunately, they often see parent's inability to sort of weigh the risk and benefit of vaccination as the most effective preventive measure.” It comes as parents like Rodriguez hope to protect her child and possibly thousands of others. “If there is something that I can prevent from my child having, especially if it's like the illness, like the measles, I will do everything in my power to be able to help him with that and prevent that from happening to him,” Rodriguez said. As this infection continues to race through pockets of unvaccinated communities, Shaw is highly advising parents to speak with their medical provider about their options, the best time frame to receive a vaccine and walk through any anxieties they may have surrounded this matter to avoid further risk later down the line

analysis.brief_en: Measles is making a concerning resurgence in the United States, with the CDC reporting 2,318 confirmed cases in 2026, the highest number in 35 years. The outbreak, particularly affecting unvaccinated communities, is driven by misinformation and declining vaccination rates. While no deaths have been reported, measles remains a highly contagious and potentially fatal disease, capable of causing severe complications like pneumonia, brain damage, and seizures. Medical experts, including Dr. Shaw from SUNY Upstate Medical University, are urging parents to ensure their children are vaccinated and to consult healthcare providers to address concerns. The resurgence is especially alarming as many younger healthcare professionals and parents have never encountered measles, potentially leading to delayed diagnosis and further transmission.

analysis.location_and_population: Affected population not specified in the evidence.
analysis.event: Traces of the measles virus were detected in multiple samples of Anchorage wastewater. The event is confirmed based on laboratory findings.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: No case count, death count, or exposure count reported. The detection indicates potential presence of measles virus in the community, but the scale of impact is not specified.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: No information provided on investigation, testing, isolation, contact tracing, prevention, treatment, or official communication. The source is a full original report, but no details about public health response are available.

analysis.brief_en: Traces of the measles virus have been detected in Anchorage wastewater over July 2026, indicating potential community transmission. The finding, confirmed through laboratory testing of wastewater samples, signals possible presence of the virus in Anchorage, though no specific case numbers or health impacts have been reported. Public health authorities have not yet disclosed details about ongoing investigations, response measures, or risk assessments. The detection underscores the utility of wastewater surveillance as an early warning tool for infectious diseases, though the full extent of the potential outbreak remains unclear pending further information.

Here’s what drivers need to know Barbecue Inn is closing — but its real story is the generations of Houstonians who made it a tradition Close Local News Texas health issues alert after 4 Montgomery County residents infected with measles Brittany Taylor, Senior Digital Content Producer Published: July 29, 2026 at 12:18 PM Tags: Texas Vaccines for Children, measles prevention, Texas Department of State Health Services, measles health alert, public health alert Texas Measles (CDC) HOUSTON – Texas health officials are warning residents and health care providers to stay alert after four cases of measles were confirmed in an unvaccinated Montgomery County family. The Texas Department of State Health Services (DSHS) issued a health alert after the family members were infected by a person with measles who traveled to Texas from another state. Recommended Videos Because measles is one of the most contagious viruses, state health officials said additional cases could occur, particularly among people who are not vaccinated. “Because measles is so contagious, additional cases could occur among unvaccinated people in the area,” DSHS said in the alert. Health officials are urging Texans to make sure they are protected by getting vaccinated with the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine. According to DSHS, two doses of the MMR vaccine are more than 97% effective at preventing measles. The vaccine is available through health care providers, and free or low-cost options are offered for eligible families through the Texas Vaccines for Children program. Pharmacists can administer the vaccine without a prescription to people 14 and older and with a prescription for children 13 and younger. What are the symptoms of measles? Symptoms typically appear seven to 21 days after exposure and often begin with: High fever Cough Runny nose Red, watery eyes A few days later, a red rash usually develops on the face before spreading to the neck, trunk and the rest of the body. People with measles are contagious from about four days before the rash appears until four days after it develops. Anyone who suspects they have measles should stay home during that time to avoid spreading the virus. What should you do if you’ve been exposed? Health officials recommend calling your health care provider before going to a doctor’s office or clinic if you believe you’ve been exposed to measles. Calling ahead allows providers to arrange testing while reducing the risk of exposing other patients. Measles spreads through coughing, sneezing or simply being near an infected person. The virus can remain in the air for up to two hours after an infected person leaves an area. While many people recover, measles can cause serious complications, including pneumonia, brain inflammation and, in some cases, death. DSHS said people with measles should seek emergency medical care if they develop difficulty breathing, severe dehydration, confusion, weakness, decreased alertness or other sudden changes in behavior. For young children, warning signs include a blue color around the mouth, crying without producing tears, severe loss of appetite or unusually low energy. analysis.brief_en: Clark County Public Health has issued a warning regarding potential measles exposure after a child with a confirmed case visited The Vancouver Clinic's Salmon Creek 1 Clinic. The alert, published on July 29, 2026, informs the public about possible exposure to the highly contagious virus. While only one confirmed case has been reported, health officials are urging potentially exposed individuals to monitor for symptoms and follow guidance. The clinic location in Salmon Creek, Clark County, is specified as the site of potential exposure. No further details about the investigation or response measures are currently available.

analysis.brief_en: State health officials in Alaska are on alert after the measles virus was detected in Anchorage. The Alaska Department of Epidemiology has issued a warning to the public following the confirmed case. No further details on the number of cases, potential exposures, or the specific response measures have been released at this time. The detection underscores the importance of vaccination and public health vigilance against highly contagious diseases like measles.

Alaska wastewater testing samples from Anchorage, Fairbanks, Eagle River and Bethel as they get prepped for processing by the state in July, 2026. Evidence of the measles virus was found in Anchorage wastewater in July, according to state epidemiologists. The data is from a national pilot program that analyzes wastewater for disease and looks for ribonucleic acid, or RNA, of certain pathogens. Joe McLaughlin, head epidemiologist for the state, said that based on those findings, "We've got at least one, maybe several people in the Anchorage sewershed catchment area that had measles around these dates, and we don't know who they were, where they were, or whether transmission was occurring." Wastewater tested positive for evidence of measles on July 7, 8, 9 and 14, but the state doesn't have comparable data yet for dates beyond mid-July. Further data is likely to come in by early August, he said. McLaughlin said officials don't know yet whether the test results are due to a traveler passing through or an Anchorage resident, but clinicians should be vigilant and on the lookout for measles. "Anybody who presents to the urgent care, the emergency department, or in for a routine clinic visit, seeing a child with an acute viral illness that's compatible with measles, they should go ahead and test them and put them in isolation if they think that they do have measles," McLaughlin said. Clayton Weingartner, who heads the wastewater analysis program for the state, said the data is thanks to a new pilot program funded by a national nonprofit organization, which uses a highly sensitive process to analyze Anchorage's wastewater. No other parts of Alaska are included in the pilot program, he said. Alaska analyzes its own wastewater too, through the Department of Environmental Conservation, a lab at the University of Alaska Anchorage and in Bethel through the Yukon-Kuskokwim Health Corporation's Office of Environmental Health. Although state testing is less sensitive, if there are more cases of measles, Weingartner said it would likely show up in the state data too. That testing is analyzed more quickly than the pilot program and can be tracked online. He said the state has detected trace amounts of measles before. "For certain pathogens like measles, which are of such high consequence, we're really working on increasing that (testing) sensitivity," he said and that the state may start notifying the public moving forward if there are trace detections. Weingartner pointed out that a person cannot get measles from wastewater, that it's a respiratory disease. And he said that while people who get the measles vaccine do shed a form of the viral RNA, the testing can differentiate what he called the "wild type" of virus versus the vaccine-derived type. "It's the wild type that we are detecting," he said. The best way to prevent measles transmission is through vaccination, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Typically, children get vaccinated before kindergarten. Symptoms for measles include a rash, high fever, a cough and congestion, tiny white spots in the mouth and red, watery eyes. If you or a family member has symptoms, McLaughlin said it's best to call a clinic before getting tested so they can prevent other patients from being exposed. Measles activity in the United States is at an all-time high since the disease was declared eliminated in the country in 2000. So, McLaughlin said it's really important for Alaskans to take precautions. "Measles could be imported from an Alaskan who's returning to Alaska from the Lower 48, or from abroad, or a tourist," he said. Measles is a very unpleasant disease to get, McLaughlin said, and long-term effects of the illness can include lifelong neurological consequences and occasionally, death. Those most at risk of hospitalization are young children and immunocompromised people. Most elders over age 60, McLaughlin said, were exposed during childhood or later vaccinated, so have immunity to the virus. Immunity through vaccination is lifelong. Arizona is part of one of the nation's largest measles outbreaks as the number of cases surpasses the record high set in 2025, with five more months of 2026 still to come. A report from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention cites more than 2,318 cases so far this year — the highest number in more than 30 years. Most of that is attributable to several major outbreaks, including a recent surge on the Arizona-Utah border. Experts have used mathematical modeling and genetic analyses to indicate the outbreak on the Utah-Arizona border could be around three to four times bigger than what’s currently known, Utah epidemiologist Dr. Leisha Nolen said. Health officials say that’s because some infections likely go unreported. The nation had 2,289 cases in 2025, the worst year for measles in more than three decades. Now, 2026 has easily become the U.S.’s worst year for measles since 1991. In addition to the significant outbreak in Utah and Arizona, an outbreak of measles in South Carolina and smaller clusters of cases in other states have sickened hundreds. In November, international health officials will meet to determine if the U.S. and Mexico have lost their measles-free status. The U.S. eliminated local measles spread in 2000 by maintaining high vaccination rates, which have fallen in recent years to below the 95% coverage needed to prevent outbreaks. Measles cases are undercounted While measles cases in the U.S. are climbing, it may be impossible to say exactly how far-reaching the spread is. Public health departments and disease researchers have long acknowledged that official counts are incomplete, because some people get sick and don’t seek out treatment — something not unique to measles. Furthermore, experts say the spread might be greater than what’s known because the virus is one of the most contagious known to medicine and vaccination rates nationwide have declined. National vaccination rates for measles, mumps and rubella — which dropped to 92.5% among kindergartners in the 2024-25 school year, from 95.2% in 2019-20 — obscure even lower rates in certain communities. In Utah, where public health officials have fought measles for more than a year, the virus has sickened more than 700 people during that time, according to the state health department. The picture is muddier in South Carolina, which had the nation’s largest outbreak in 35 years. There, the 997 total is likely an undercount, the state health department has said, but it doesn’t know by how much. KNAU and Arizona News Measles virus detected in Sedona wastewater samples Bree Burkitt Samples from the Sedona Wastewater Treatment Plant tested positive for the measles virus. That indicates that at least one person with a recent infection has been in the area. Listen • 0:43 Dr. Brannon Traxler, acting director of the state department of health, said the undercount is “impossible to know and may vary during the course of an outbreak.” Data gaps can make it hard to reliably estimate an outbreak’s true scope. Experts say hospitalization rates can be a good barometer, but measles hospitalizations are not required to be reported in every state. “If we really had some kind of solid gold standard for the percentage of all cases that have hospitalization or some measure of severity, then that would be another way of estimating the outbreak size that we could see if it’s consistent with these other methods,” said Damon Toth, an applied mathematician at the University of Utah’s medical school who is working on one of the Utah outbreak analyses. Researchers are still analyzing the 2025 Texas outbreak In Texas, researchers are still working to estimate the size of the state’s 2025 outbreak and early findings show it might have been nearly twice the size of the 762 known cases. Rémy Pasco, a mathematical epidemiologist at the University of Colorado Boulder who is working on the analysis, said the undercounts were unsurprising. In the absence of an adequate community vaccination rate — 95% according to health experts — “there’s just not much you can do about measles once you have it,” he said. The CDC defines an outbreak as three or more linked cases. But by the time three such cases are identified in communities with low vaccination rates and less disease surveillance, “either you missed the previous ones or you’re going to have a lot more,” he added. Dr. Varun Shetty, Texas’ chief state epidemiologist, said there were instances where people tested positive for measles but health officials couldn’t confirm who else was in the person’s household or if they were sick. “What we’re able to count and report is almost always an underestimate of what actually occurred, because it relies on people being willing to be able to get tested, to share information with healthcare providers and with public health,” Shetty said. “Sometimes that just doesn’t happen.” The state health department previously reported that 182 probable measles cases went unconfirmed in March 2025 among minors in Gaines County — the epicenter of the outbreak — due to a lack of information. The confirmed case count for the western Texas county for the whole outbreak is 414. Shetty expects to keep seeing measles cases and even outbreaks because so many people are unprotected. “It’s really critical, not only for individual people, but for communities, to have high vaccination coverage,” he said. Vaccination is about protecting others, physician says Dr. Mark Roberts, retired director of the Public Health Dynamics Lab at the University of Pittsburgh School of Public Health, worries most for the people he calls “innocent bystanders.” Research and measles modeling by his team shows those who cannot get vaccinated — young babies, people with weak immune systems and those who rarely don’t get robust immunity from the vaccine — bear the brunt of outbreaks early on. Some people see skipping vaccination as like deciding not to wear a seat belt in a car, Roberts said. “Not vaccinating your kid is like saying, ‘I don’t want my car to have brakes,’” he said. “Because it’s other people that you can hit. It’s not just you in your car. It’s other people.” KNAU and Arizona News Unmapped Route 66: Starlite Lanes thrives as the Mother Road celebrates centennial Adrian Skabelund For seven decades, Flagstaff’s Starlite Lanes has been a bowling beacon in the Flagstaff community along Route 66. Now, its owner looks to pass the torch to the next generation.
